[10/16/20, 1:41:10 PM] ‪+1 (928) 600‑6331‬: As we start with shabbos beraishis this week just sharing in case it helps: 

Many times we struggle with finding a good message to give over to our students at Friday night. Part of the challenge is that its really hard to get their attention to focus and tune in, especially when there is a big crowd in one room - and even when its outdoors now with covid with everyone spread out. 

So Over the years I tried to transition into giving over each week a “Story of the Week”. Its usually a short 2-3 min story that always has before it a short vort/idea connected to the parsha that is relevant for their own lives. I find that they pay much more attention and are really tuned in as when I get up to give my weekly Message they are expecting and waiting for this weeks story. 

Being that time is short I don’t write it up this week however I have been recording them as a short voice note to share with fellow shluchim who may find it helpful. Its usually bet 3-5 min (not more than that). If you are interested in recieving it each week to give you an idea for your shabbat dinner message let me know and Ill add you to the weekly whatsapp broadcast where i send out the voice note. Hatzlacha!

It was discussed on this chat a while ago regarding Walmart corporate grants. I was recently approved for a grant and It can be quite simple. There is a simple online form to fill out. 
The way it works is that the store manager in each facility is the one that is able to approve your grant. Highly recommended to meet them first before applying. Otherwise you will most likely not be getting it.

Here is a recording of a conference call with Avi Rubinfeld explaining how to go about it.

https://fccdl.in/fPJeuovfB2

[11/5/20, 9:16:36 PM] ‪+1 (323) 545‑7642‬: By Rabbi Dovid Sholom Pape

 I want to share with you a story that happened 38 years ago.

My wife and I were then with Chabad in Buffalo.

Like most cities in America, in Buffalo, there are no corner stores. If you need to do some shopping, you have to go to the mall. And so, one day, my wife and I got in the car to go to Wegman’s, a large supermarket.

A lot of people pass through Buffalo on their way to Niagara Falls, or other places in Canada. Often they call Chabad and ask if there is a place where they can stay for Shabbos. This happens a lot. I remember, when it lived in London, it was the same. People were always passing through on their way to other destinations, and needed a place to stay for a day or two.

Just that morning, some people had complained about this kind of behavior. They felt that it wasn’t right to have such an attitude. They said that people were just taking advantage, and should just be directed to the nearest hotel.

I mentioned this conversation to my wife, and said that it didn’t seem right to me. After all, why were we in Buffalo if not to be of help to others? Wasn’t that why the Rebbe had sent us?

We had hardly gone two or three minutes, when I noticed that we needed gas, and turned into the gas station on the corner.

As I got out to open the gas tank, a man in his fifties got out of his car and began walking towards me. I noticed that he reached in his back pocket and pulled out a yarmulke.

“Shalom,” he greeted me with a smile. “Do you know where I can find a hotel?”

I could tell from his accent that he was Israeli.

‘Hashem,’ I said to myself. ‘Are you testing me? I just finished talking to my wife about this.’

“Just a minute,” I replied, turning back to speak to my wife again.

Rabbi Dworkin ע''ה used to say that a person shouldn’t bring guests home without permission from his wife, and vice versa.

“Shulamit,” I said, “this man just asked me where he could find a hotel. Can we invite him to stay with us?”

“Absolutely,” she agreed at once.

I turned back to him. “Why don’t you come and stay with us?”  I said.

“Oh no, we couldn’t do that,” he said. “That’s very kind of you, but there are four of us. We couldn’t all stay with you. Please just tell me where there is a hotel. We only need to stay one night.”

“Just a minute,” I said, laughing to myself. ‘Hashem, are You upping the stakes?’

I turned back to my wife. “He’s says there are four of them. Can we handle that?”

“Not a problem,” she replied.

Well, it took some convincing to get him to agree, but in the end he did agree, and we turned around and brought the whole lot back to our apartment. We only had two bedrooms, but with a couch and two cots, it worked out fine. One of them had an aunt who lived nearby. And one of them slept on a blanket on the carpet.

What should I say? They were the nicest people. We had a wonderful time together. They were all musicians on their way to perform a concert in Toronto for Yom Ha-Atzme’ut. A father, and two sons, a son-in-law, and a drummer. We talked and talked till the wee hours, late at night. They were full of questions about the Rebbe, and were thirsty to hear stories about him. I remember telling them an amazing story I had heard from Rabbi Nachman Sudak ע''ה, about Arik Sharon and the Rebbe before the Yom Kippur war. And how, when he came out of yechidus with the Rebbe, he said to the bochurim,  “Boys, as great as you think your Rebbe is, you don’t know even a bit of what he really is.”

The next day we all got up early and went to the Chabad House for shachris. They helped make the minyan. So everyone was grateful for that. When we came back for breakfast, the father went out and bought a tricycle at a garage sale for our 2 year old son. During bentching, they added in a lot of personal brochos for us, and especially for my wife who was in her seventh month.

It was a wonderful experience. We parted on the best of terms.

Six months later I came to New York to be at the big farbrengen for Yud Tess Kislev. As I stood there, waiting for the farbrengen to start, I felt a tap on my shoulder. It was the younger brother. “Do you remember me?” he said. “I am here now! Yes. I started learning here in Crown Heights in the Yeshiva Hadar HaTorah. My brother is in Queens, and all the family are getting more involved in Yiddishkeit! All because of the night we spent in your house.”

After that, Baruch Hashem, their lives developed in a very positive way as they became more and more involved with Chabad and the Rebbe, eventually getting married, and having families.

We remained best of friends till the present day.

In their careers as musicians, they met with great success, and their relationship with Chabad and the Rebbe has played a very important role, and has had a powerful influence on Jewish music. Every year on Succos, thousands upon thousands of people rejoice and dance to the joyous music of Yossi and Avi Piamenta. 

That’s their story. It all started from the Mitzvah of Hachnassos Orchim.

For many years, Avi has asked me to write it up. I thought this week it would be appropriate.

[11/9/20, 6:31:41 PM] Levi Begun: Someone posted a how to from home Depot
----
Sharing incase it’s helpful to anyone as it seems car menorah parades will be a popular thing this year. These menorahs we made together with a local electrician friend out of pvc pipe, it’s not a difficult project and comes out cheaper then buying menorahs.

The design was based off of this site - https://biblebeltbalabusta.com/2011/11/02/pvc-menorah-advice-needed/amp/

And if you want to do the easier route you can order these candles instead of running electricity through it - https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07X7CVQRN/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_api_i_.amOFbMWE78ZZ?_encoding=UTF8&psc=1

We also spray painted them silver to give it a more real look. 

Total cost is between $25-30 a menorah

[11/11/20, 7:07:27 PM] ‪+1 (646) 717‑3279‬: *רשימת שינויי השמות*

רשימת השמות לועזים שהרבי החליף – רשימה חלקית – מקובץ "זורע צדקות", יומנים, עדיות מאנשים.

א)      האשה ביקשה שהרבי יתן לה שם יהודי. כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א: "מה שמך כעת?"הנ"ל: אליס.  כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א התפלא, והיא חזרה שוב על השם הנ"ל. הרלי"ג חזר באופן ברור יותר. כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א נענע קצת בראשו הק', ואמר שיהי' שמה "עליה".

האשה לא הבינה, ואמר כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א: "עיי"ן, למ"ד, יו"ד, ה"א", והגביה ידו עם הדולר (והראה בידו) ואמר "עליה", והוסיף (באנגלית) "עליה מתמידה כל הזמן".
ב)      לבנם שביקש שם יהודי (להנ"ל יש שם יהודי אלא שלא רגיל להשתמש בו), והאם אמרה ששמו הוא צ'רלס, כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א הביט בתמיהה קצת והריל"ג חזר על השם. הת' שהציגם אמר שיש לו שם יהודי – "דוד". כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א נתן דולר נוסף באמרו: "דוד – תשים דולר זה בקופת הצדקה".



ג)       לאשה ששמה שביקשה עבור בתה ששמה מישל שם יהודי אמר כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א: יש שם בלשון הקודש "מיכל" – מ"ם, יו"ד, כ"ף, למ"ד, והשי"ת יברך אותך.



ד)      לאשה שביקשה שם יהודי עבור בתה בהוסיפה ששמה ברוסית הוא עינגא אמר כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א: "עינגא" – אין זה שם רוסי. הנ"ל: נתנו לה שם זה על שם אביה יצחק. כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א: אם כך תני לה שם כפי שאשתו של יצחק נקראה – רבקה. שיקראו לה "רבקה", ושהיה בשעה טובה.  כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א (לבת): שיהיו לך חיים ארוכים ושמחים כרבקה.



ה)      CLAIR  * לאשה ששמה האנגלי קלייר ובקשה שם יהודי. כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א: שתתן שם שמתחיל אף הוא בקו"ף. שיהיה "קריינא". והוסיף "קריינא' מיינט 'קראון' ["קריינא" משמעותו כתר}.

[11/17/20, 1:29:31 PM] ‪+44 7710 524460‬: Dear Friend,

It is my great pleasure to present you with our second community magazine, produced locally, in honour of Chanukah.
Chanukah is a holiday of many messages and lessons, and is a most welcome holiday in this strange time we find ourselves in.
Thinking over the story, I cannot help but imagine what they must have felt upon finding the small, untouched cruise of oil with which to light the Menorah.
Just picture for yourself how powerful that moment must have been. After a bruising victory, the small group of faithful Jews returns to the Temple, only to find it completely ransacked and defiled.
“Is it possible?”, they surely pondered; “Can we rebuild? The Temple needs to be completely refurbished. The majority of our brethren have forsaken the faith. Can we restore the Temple and our kingdom to its former glory?”
Then, they found that small jug still sealed with the seal of the high priest from before the Greek conquest. And they knew the answer.
They knew that they would be able to rebuild. Because the Jewish spirit can never be destroyed nor diminished. All you need to do is find that little bit of oil and with it you can light a giant Menorah whose light will continue to shine for thousands of years.
So as you light your Menorah/Chanukiyah each night of Chanukah, I encourage you to think of just how long these small flames have lasted, how many thousands of years of difficulty and persecution they have witnessed, and how fortunate we are to keep them burning today. 
May the lights of Chanukah continue to illuminate and be a source of warmth, so that once these 8 days are gone, all that they represent carries on. 
Happy, Healthy Chanukah!

[11/20/20, 12:07:47 PM] ‪+1 (917) 983‑6715‬: A FEVER OF FRIENDSHIP

Well, this is interesting. 

Last week was supposed to be the annual conference of Shluchim (Chabad rabbis) in New York. Since that couldn't happen, the conference moved online. Workshops, break-out sessions, presentations - everything virtual.

For Motzai Shabbat (Saturday night) the organizers arranged for a Farbrengen on Zoom that would begin in Australia where Shabbat ends earliest. As Shabbat gradually ended in other time zones, more regions joined the Farbrengen. It was a beautiful way to spend Saturday night.

But then a funny thing happened - it didn't end Saturday night. In fact, it still hasn't ended. Since Saturday night, over 120 hours ago, this Farbrengen has rolled along, orbiting the globe and bringing good cheer, great stories and plenty of Lchaims as it goes. (Without intending to, it has set the record for longest Zoom meeting, easily bringing down the previous record of 24 hours.) As the Shluchim in one part of the world start falling asleep, another group wakes up and the Fabrengen is seamlessly handed over to them.

It's completely informal. At one point, the Shliach in Norway acted the MC role; then Minnesota took over; then New Mexico; then Liverpool. People from Ashdod to South Korea to Montevideo are sharing cherished memories of the Rebbe. Others are telling tales from their Chabad House life. Others are toasting everyone with Lchaims and good wishes. Smiles are aplenty, jokes too; it's like a giant, endless, virtual class reunion. Due to Zoom limitations, maximum participation is 1,000 people, and it's too small to accommodate everyone, G-d bless them all.

One of the speakers, Rabbi Yudi Dukes, spoke from his hospital bed, where he is recovering from coronavirus. He mentioned this idea:

"Everyone knows that on Sukkot, when we gather up the Lulav, Etrog, Hadas and Aravot, it symbolizes the unity of our People. Though the species are each unique, they come together in friendship in G-d's service. But what many people do not realize is that each species on it's own is a symbol of unity. For example, the Lulav is a branch with numerous leaves that are all stuck together, like diverse people uniting together, and the Etrog is a fruit that flourishes in every season, finding the blessings in every condition, like a person who finds the beauty in everyone. And it is only because they contain unity in themselves that they are able to spread unity around them and bring people together."

This point brought home the true greatness of this endless, global Farbrengen. The secret of Chabad's contribution to the Jewish world - the unprecedented Jewish unity and camaraderie generated by all the Chabad Houses - is not Chabad's efficiancy. It is not Chabad's marketing. It is not Chabad's non-judgmentalism. Rather, the reason Chabad creates friendship and brotherhood between others is because Chabad's personnel - the Shluchim - is a large, jolly group of friends.

If the Shluchim were "colleagues," they would create colleagues. If they were "members" of an elite club, they would create "members." If they were "outreach professionals," they would create "professional Jews." 

But because the Shluchim of the world are a huge group of friends, they create friends. Because they feel like brothers, they make Jews feel like family.

One thousand rabbis, in one thousand locations, separated by oceans and joined by computer screens, joked and shmoozed and sang and laughed and cried together; an intimate handful of one thousand buddies.

Lead by a Rebbe who was utterly at one within himself, with his G-d and his People, Chabad contracted the Rebbe's fever of friendship and thank G-d, it has spread like a pandemic to every corner of the Jewish world, and beyond.

This friendship and this brotherhood was palpable every year at the conference in New York. But this year, during this thrilling, exciting, week-long Farbrengen, the closeness was more palpable than ever.

Sure we Jews are a Nation, a People, a religion. But more than anything, we are an intimate handful of friends, brothers and sisters, part of the global Jewish family bringing friendship and camaraderie to the whole, wide world. May G-d grant that every Jew in the world catch this fever of friendship, and feel a part of this family.

Good Shabbos, Shabbat Shalom!

Rabbi Eli Friedman
Chabad of Calabasas

P.S. A real friendship is a lifeline not only for the friends, but for everyone they know, and everyone who knows them. During these times, friendships may falter; let this mass Zoom Farbrengen inspire everyone to realize that friendships are possible, palpable, and can still serve as a warm blessing to everyone around. Spread the friendship fever and bring your friends back together!

[12/2/20, 5:08:17 PM] ‪+61 450 095 828‬: *From Merkos suite 302.*

Dear Shliach,

The energy of the kinus is still in the air and although it looked and felt different this year its unique kind of inspiration still lives on.

At the height of the unprecedented global Zoom farbrengen, there was a moment of revelation as a group of shluchim pondered out loud, “What if we share this energy and palpable feeling of unity with the rest of the world?”

Indeed, how special it would be if we gave Jews from the entire world this feeling of empowerment, identity and connection that they are a part of something greater.

After the record setting Zoom farbrengen ended, it was time to turn this dream into fruition.

The idea: A Global Chanukah landing site featuring shluchim and celebrations from around the world, around the clock. A Chanukah party marathon set to be the longest and largest in the world. 

Imagine the feeling of a lonely Jew sitting isolated at home, somewhat dejected that he can’t celebrate properly, and then the overwhelming feeling of joy he experiences when he discovers that in truth he is not alone as he participates in a Menorah lighting broadcast from hundreds of miles away, engulfing him with a sense of belonging and pride. He knows that no matter the circumstance, time and place, language or culture, we the Jewish people are celebrating Chanukah together.

Do you share this vision? Would you like your Chanukah event broadcast on such a program?

Are you ready for ‘Chanukah Together’?

All you need to do is commit to airing your Chanukah celebration for half an hour and sharing it with the world. Your community will feel honored to be featured across the globe, and that one lonely Jew may find just what she is looking for by tuning in to your program.

‘Chanukah Together’ will kick-off on Sunday, December 13th with a 12 hour ‘Chanukah Live’ style program in conjunction with a major TV station and then continue onward until the last day of Chanukah for an impressive 100 plus hours of constant Chanukah celebration.

Help create a modern Chanukah miracle and keep the flame and message burning for 8 days straight!

Please take a moment to fill out the form so we can determine the next steps in making this vision a reality.

https://merkos302.formstack.com/forms/chanukahtogether

[12/16/20, 6:56:43 AM] Yaakov Koppel Chaiton: This Chanukah - Chabad Jewish Center salutes our heroes!

Today we share this holiday, its message and some traditional treats with you in celebration. It is our small way of letting you know - We think of you and pray for the health and safety of you and your family.

Why the doughnut?

(Well of course they taste great!)

The miracle of the Chanukah story centers around oil, more specifically olive oil.
When the Jewish Holy Temple was desecrated by the occupying Greek armies, the Jews stood up for their beliefs and bravely chased them out. When they returned to the Temple they could only find one small flask of oil that could burn for only one night but miraculously it burned for eight straight nights..


We therefore celebrate Chanukah by eating foods fried in oil such as potato patties or doughnuts.

The holiday of Chanuka also stands for freedom of religion and the need to rise above anti-Semitism and hate.
A few brave heroes demonstrated that light and goodness will always overpower darkness and hate. Regardless of the personal costs of thier actions, they each knew that was something greater at stake; something worth sacrificing everything for.

Today we also have such heroes!
It is each one of you who put yourselves on the line selflessly day in and day out to help others.

YOU, the members of the Police and Fire Department, members of the EMS and our soldiers on land and sea, do this for anyone and everyone regardless of ethnicity, religion or background.

On behalf of the entire community - Thank you and G-d bless.

Warmly,

[12/25/20, 4:08:47 PM] Chaim Markovits Chaim Hillel: Written by Rabbi Eliyahu Schusterman from Atlanta 


I received two thank you calls today from Shluchim who I have coached in past years. At the time I encouraged them to connect with a therapist to address frustrations and issues that they were dealing with that negatively affected their Shlichus, their Shalom bayis and their own well being.  Normal, regular Shluchim just like you and me.

They called to thank me for encouraging them to do the therapy as it has changed their lives.  Of course the Chabad house structure, fundraising, time management etc. were also important but the therapy gave them the peace of mind and direction they needed to be present in their Chabad Houses.

In light of recent tragic events, I must speak out and encourage any Shlach here who is struggling with any issue (you don't have to be struggling with addictions, or severe mental health issues to need therapy) that is negatively affecting your Shalom bayis, your sleep, your ability to be effective at your Shlichus; PLEASE SEEK HELP.  There is no shame in it and it will liberate you and you will be a happier person for it.  

If I can be of any service to you in this regard, please don't hesitate to text me.  Good Shabbos and all my love and blessings. Eliyahu

ב"ה, ט' תמוז, תשט"ז
ברוקלין.
שלום וברכה!
במענה על מכתבו - בלי הוראת זמן הכתיבה - בו כותב על שמקטנותו התרועע עם נער אחד יתום, אבל אח"כ גבה טורא ביניהו והנ"ל נתרחק מהסביבה החרדית בה נתחנכו ונתגדלו וכו', ויודע שעתה מסתובב הוא בסביבה חפשית, ומתייעץ בעצמו איך להשפיע עליו וכו'.
ופלא הקור רוח בו נכתב כל הנ"ל, אף שהדבר נוגע בהצלת נפש אחת מישראל לחיי העולם הבא וגם לחיי העולם הזה, וגודל ענין כזה אין צריך ביאור, ומובן ופשוט שבהקדם האפשרי עליו להתחיל בהשפעה על האמור באופן הכי יעיל אשר לא כל האישים והמצבים שוים בזה כמובן, אבל בודאי כשיתייעץ בזה עם אלו הנמצאים על אתר והמכירים בתנאי המצב ויטכסו עצה ויקוים כמ"ש ותשועה ברוב יועץ, וההקדם בכל זה ישובח וגם מוכרח, כיון שכל רגע וכל יום הם אבדה שאינה חוזרת, וכבר ידוע פסק תוה"ק לעולם יראה עצמו שקול וכל העולם כולו שקול וע"י ענין אחד יכול להכריע עצמו וכל העולם לכף זכות וכו' ובהתבוננות קלה שההכרעה יכולה להיות ממש ברגע ודוחה הפעולה מאיזה סיבה שתהי', הרי תסמרנה שערות הראש מהתוצאות האפשריות מדיחוי זה, והאריכות בזה אך למותר, ויהי רצון שכאמור יתחיל תיכף בפעולה ההתחלה עכ"פ ויהי' בהצלחה.
בטח יודע משלשת השיעורים השוים לכל נפש מתקנת כ"ק מו"ח אדמו"ר
זצוקללה"ה נבג"מ זי"ע בחומש תהלים ותניא הידועים, וישמור אותם עכ"פ מכאן ולהבא.
בברכה,
בשם כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א

Sharing my experience hoping it helps calm someone's nerves.

January first was a hard day for me.

I felt so lost about 2021.

I had to start again from scratch. No more "we've raised $35,000 towards our budget can you help with a gift of x?" I felt like I had nothing to build from.

I wasn't sure where to start, and looking at the numbers to compare from last year felt overwhelming.

I do have Mendy Teldons sheet. But kept delaying.

Last week I stopped pushing things off and started working.

Some people gave for Chanukah.

There's no reason to assume they won't want to give again for Purim.

And High Holidays.

And next year Chanukah too.

I started putting the "hopeful" numbers in.

For every single donation. Even people who gave $5 for a high holiday or Chanukah package they received.



It took me five hours.

But when I was done it felt so good.

I had a possible path to over 90% of our budget.

The calming feeling that I have a strategy to follow.

But more calming was the realization.

That I can't control who will end up giving what.

But I can show Hashem that I'm serious about making keilim.

[1/21/21, 7:56:18 AM] Zalmen Ives: Two thieves came down a chimney... Not so quick, but really describes Talmud in a humorous way.
[1/21/21, 8:03:21 AM] ‪+1 (818) 826‑0851‬: I don’t have a joke, but there’s a great intro I once heard to explain basic Talmud premises:

There was a rabbi who got up at the Bimah after Kol Nidrei and announced to his congregation: “everyone remember that tonight is Yom Kippur. We cannot eat or drink”. A newcomer in the back starts shouting “Not true. I clearly remember my grandfather standing in a Kittel and announcing that you’re not allowed to eat but you’re allowed to drink!”

The Rabbi calls him over and tries explaining to him about Yom Kippur but the guy takes none of it. He insists on the memory of his grandfather’s announcement. Until the Rabbi understood what happened. This guy was remembering the end of the Seder night after the afikoman, when you can’t eat but are allowed to drink...

Very helpful anecdote to explain the concept of הכא במאי עסקינן which is a major premise in גמ׳, you have two Rabbis insisting on opposing statements, and it’s easily rectified by assigning each statement to a different case.

[1/21/21, 6:55:44 PM] ‪+1 (214) 734‑7282‬: Seems I opened a discussion here...

But just to give a few thoughts about it as I have an advisor and I do have a whole life policy along with a term (and something else). Maybe it will help someone. Of course there are many schools of thoughts in this area. 


From my understanding there a few advantages to them:

First off yes they are more expensive than a term but they also will grow your money unlike a term.  
And you only pay into for a set amount of years then it’s over you own it and it continues to grow even after you stop paying. 

And the two big points are 
1- it’s a tax haven which means when you use money from it it is not taxable (because you are borrowing from your policy) this could be important for families that need to stay under a income threshold to get other benefits.
2- when you do take out the policy continues to grow as if that money is still in there and if you want you can put back the money. 

Anyway if you want to hear real numbers you can message me and id be happy to share with you. 

But yes get term before all else!!

Bez”h no one will need to collect and the amount paid will only be there for peace of mind.

[1/22/21, 2:06:05 AM] ‪+1 (716) 650‑0613‬: BH

*The inaugural address of a new era*

The inaugural address is an opportunity for the new president to share a message that will hopefully shape the imminent future and serve as an inspiration for generations to come. Although at times these speeches produced memorable quotes, rarely are they considered to be the dawn of a new era.

Seventy years ago, on the 10th day of Shevat 1951, exactly one year after the Previous Rebbe’s passing, the Rebbe led a Chassidic gathering in which it was believed he would formally accept the mantle of Chabad Lubavitch leadership. For many months, hundreds of Chassidim had petitioned him to assume the official title of “Lubavitcher Rebbe,” although he informally assumed most of the responsibilities of the position almost immediately.

The Chassidim were waiting for the Rebbe to deliver a “Maamer” - an original Chassidic discourse - which is the exclusive privilege and duty of the “Lubavitcher Rebbe.” On that Wednesday evening, the Rebbe delivered his inaugural discourse - called “Bosi Legani” - to the immense joy and relief of Chassidim around the world and changed the course of Jewish history.

Within a decade of the horrors of the Holocaust, as millions of Jews - including most of the Chabad community - remained trapped behind the iron curtain, the Rebbe spoke of a new era. Instead of issuing poetic and aspirational statements, the Rebbe gleaned from multiple sources in Talmud and Jewish mysticism to illustrate that the feasibility of fulfilling our mission to perfect the world, and the urgency to do so in our time, is a proven fact.

Whereas everyone in the room that evening had lost so much and felt so broken - the Rebbe announced that each and every one of them could change the world for good in ways their ancestors could not fathom. Whereas everyone else saw the physical destruction of our nation and the onslaught of assimilation - the Rebbe declared that specifically our generation would complete the historic task of perfecting our world with the arrival of Moshiach.

He spoke of Avraham the first Jew who dedicated his life to enlightening a heathen civilization with the light of monotheism. Avraham worked tirelessly to inspire others to become teachers of this truth as well, the Rebbe explained, and this remains the ultimate prototype for Jewish success to this day: if you want to be Jewish, you must share your Jewishness with others.

Most importantly, perfecting the world is our mandate and destiny not because of our superior talents or elevated spiritual status, but rather simply because we are alive today.

Amazingly there is a recording of that historic event and as I listened to it this evening the Rebbe’s words sounded more relevant today than ever before. We’ve come a long way since 1951, but the world is not yet perfect and the urgency to complete our mission only intensifies with time.

This Shabbat is the 10th of Shevat. As we celebrate 71 years of the Rebbe’s leadership and 70 years from his inaugural discourse,  I encourage you to dedicate more time to studying Torah and to share your knowledge with others. Observe a new Mitzvah and encourage a friend to do the same. Increase your Tzedakah giving (before or after Shabbat) and inspire others to give as well. Because each act of kindness makes this world a better place and hastens the arrival of Moshiach when goodness, peace and freedom will abound for all.

[1/22/21, 3:12:50 PM] ‪+1 (330) 861‑8770‬: *Where will you be this Shabbos?*

I don’t (just) mean geographically, I mean your focus and attitude.

What am I asking?  

Let me explain.

***

Something absolutely amazing was shared on a recent zoom by a first-hand witness (Rabbi Levi Garelik):

In anticipation of “Celebration 40” of the Rebbe’s Nesius in 1990 Rabbi Yossi Hecht of Johannesburg, SA asked his father, the legendary Rabbi J.J. Hecht, to come to South Africa as guest speaker for the grand farbrengen for yud shevat 40 years. 

As with everything, Rabbi Hecht asked the Rebbe what to do, if he should go or not. 

The Rebbe responded (Rabbi Garelik personally saw the answer):

*"עד עכשיו שמעתי שבאים לכאן לחגוג שנת הארבעים"*
Loosely translated: 
*Until now I have heard that [people are] coming here for the 40th year [celebration]*

Think about it for a moment.

Rabbi Hecht isn’t asking if he should leave for a family simchah or “vacation”... 
he is asking if he should travel to a community to inspire them! 

And yet - the Rebbe says that he should better remain (with him - the Rebbe) for this celebration.

***

Everyone will translate this story in different ways.

Here is how one simple Jew took it:

There are moments the Rebbe wants us to be with him.
Plain and simple. 
To celebrate with him. 
To appreciate him and all he gives us.

***

This year most of us won’t be able to be in the physical daled amos of the Rebbe - but I believe we CAN “be with the Rebbe” over Shabbos and Sunday. 

Not only by doing our shlichus with whomever we come in contact with of course.

But also, in these final moments of “Shnas Hashiviim” - and in these moments of world turbulence in so many ways, on so many levels - by pausing over Shabbos to internalize all the Rebbe gives us.

As the Rebbe once said in a Bosi Legani Maamer (5730) “מ’גיסט און מ’גיסט און מ’גיסט”, “we “pour” and “pour” and “pour”...”

Internalizing in our hearts and minds, and yes, verbalizing, to ourselves, to our spouses, and our children - Ashreinu Mah Tov Chelkeinu!

How lucky we are to be in the Rebbe’s generation.
How lucky we are that in these moments of utter chaos and confusion we have a Rebbe with a clarion call and mandate.
A Rebbe that teaches us how to approach every event, interaction, and relationship.
A Rebbe that continues to shower us with blessings of all sorts and hold our hands through thick and thin.

May we be appropriate vessels for those blessings
May we have the wisdom and heart to appreciate and internalize all we have been given and continue to receive
May we be blessed with the energy to materialize that which is demanded of us
Most importantly: may we merit most immediately to see the Rebbe with our physical eyes - now!

[Adai Ad - Just One Thing]
*THANK YOUR SPOUSE. OFTEN.*

Think of the little and big things that your spouse brings to your life and family. Thank them. With a full gratitude.  Don’t anything for granted, as if it is their job.
  
*When you are gracious in your thinking, you will think of lots of things to be grateful for.* “Thank you for taking care of the baby so I could get a full night sleep. I feel so energetic this morning.”  “Thank you for always having my favorite snacks (fruits) stocked.” “Thank you for making us laugh so often.”

Share your gratitude often and freely. You might make a master list of things for which you are grateful, and pull from that list when you are not remembering what you can share your gratitude about. 
- 
If you don’t ask much from your spouse (for whatever reason), begin to ask.  Your spouse wants to make you happy, wants to contribute to your life. Sometimes, they just don’t know what it is that you want or need. “I’m feeling stressed. Can you please make me a cup of tea – the mint tea, with one spoon of sugar.”

Ask clearly and graciously – not nagging, not demanding, not hinting. Don’t not ask because they ‘should know what I want’ or they ‘should know what needs to be done’.

*Ask, so that they can give. Ask, so that they do for you and the family and then you have what to ground your gratitude on.*

www.adaiad.org
https://www.facebook.com/AdaiAdInstitute
https://www.instagram.com/adai_ad

to subscribe for daily tips - http://bitly.com/subscribe-AdaiAd-JOT

Megillah
Matonos Levyonim
Mishloach Manos

After tzeis, eat another kzayis of bread.
Al nissim and rtzei in benching
Kabbolas Shabbos / Maariv

[2/8/21, 3:02:27 PM] ‪+1 (412) 708‑2734‬: B"H

Dear {{first name}},

Thank you for your recent gift of {{amount}} to Valley Chabad. Thank you for supporting Valley Chabad with your generous gift. Thank you for being a friend and creating blessings for the VC community!!!

Purim is in the air :)

Do you remember when children and adults wearing masks meant it was Purim? When covering our faces signaled in the happy and joyous day of sharing gifts and celebrating friendships?

The  masked world of today has forced the world to look deeper, beyond the surface. Norms have been challenged, smiles have been covered over and the unknown continues to linger.

In the Purim story, the heroes were Mordechai and Queen Esther.

Today, YOU are the hero. 

You are the hero who looks beyond the surface and brings joy and care to a community in need of friendship and inspiration. 

Purim food gifts and charity demonstrate the true nature of the extended family known as the Jewish people.

Your thoughtful support of Valley Chabad demonstrates the true nature of our local Jewish family. Thank you for caring and taking action.

The world has changed. The needs have changed. The way we interact has changed.

Your friendship has NOT changed!!!

Thank you for all you are doing at this time of greater need. My prayers and best wishes for good health, good news and happy times all around.

Happy Purim to you and your dear family,
Rabbi Dov

[2/9/21, 8:01:01 PM] ‪+1 (323) 770‑3433‬: Any templates or resources on helping write up a Bar Mitzva speech with a Bar Mitzva boy?
[2/9/21, 8:05:30 PM] ‪+1 (224) 392‑4442‬: I have this as my basic generic BM speech downloaded from shluchim exchange a while ago
[2/9/21, 8:05:53 PM] ‪+1 (224) 392‑4442‬: Good Morning everyone and Thank you for joining me today as I celebrate my Bar Mitzvah. 

 I am lucky to have grown up and been educated by my parents. One thing I have learned from them is that just being Jewish is not enough, in order to be a proud Jew, we must act Jewish as well. 

I would like to thank my parents for teachig me and guiding me in the proper fashion especially since they both come from countries where acting Jewish was a terrible crime. I thank my parents for not just teaching me, but encouraging me and being a living example of what it means to be a good person, a Mentsch, and a good Jew.  

I have been preparing for this day for many weeks now and I’d like to share some of the very interesting things that I have learned about what becoming a Jewish man means. I would also like to share with you all some cool facts about the special mitzvah of Tefillin.

Bar Mitzvah literally means "a son of the Mitzvot." On the day of one’s Bar or Bat Mitzvah a young boy or girl matures into a full-fledged member of the Jewish people. On this day, they become responsible for their own actions and obligated to perform all of the mitzvot in the Torah (G-d’s commandments).  

Two of the mitzvot that are most identified with a Bar Mitzvah boy are: Being called up to the Torah and putting on Tefillin. The Hebrew word Torah is related to the word Ho-ra-ah which means “lesson.” The Torah is meant to be a set of guidelines and serve as the blueprint of how we should live our lives. We are not supposed to just learn the Torah on surface level, but we are supposed to glean actual lessons from everything we learn and incorporate them into our daily lives.

Mitzvot, can only be performed down here in this physical world. The whole idea of a mitzvah is to bring down G-dliness into the physical – into the world of action. When we perform mitzvot, we connect with Hashem and this connection actually affects not just us but the world around us, elevating and perfecting the world and making our world a dwelling place for Hashem. 

The mitzvah of Tefillin is the Mitzvah to wrap special leather straps on the arm, facing the heart and to place it on the head. There are many symbols and life lessons in the mitzvah of Tefillin which really tell us the importance of all Torah and Mitzvot.

For example, the Tefillin straps are black which teach us that G-d’s ways are hidden and there are things in life that we will encounter that will not always be understood, an important and timeless life lesson. 

The three headed shin and four headed shin on each side of the Tefillin reminds us of our three forefathers and our four mothers, teaching us that we must always look to our elders for guidance and instruction.

The tefillin are made out of products that come from a kosher animal. This teaches us that while perfecting ourselves must come through physical labor and refining our natural, animalistic behaviors, that refinement must be achieved in a positive and permissible way for a Jew.

We place Tefillin on our arm and head, reminding us that all of our actions done with our hands must be done for the sake of Heaven and all of our emotions must be controlled by our mind.

Finally, the Tefillin is a square shape-a man made shape, symbolizing that the the ultimate goal of creation which is to bring the world into a sense of perfection where G-dliness and physicality are in sync, is a goal which can only be achieved by man.

As I become a link in the chain of our almost 4,000 year history, I accept upon myself this responsibility of bridging the gap between the physical and the G-dly. I will try to lead by example; putting on Tefillin each day and performing the mitzvot that I am now obligated to fulfill.

I hope and pray that in the merit of all our combined mitzvot and good deeds; Hashem will watch and protect our sisters and brothers in the Holy Land of Israel and throughout the entire world. May G-d grant the entire world Shalom (peace) now and forever with the coming of Moshiach speedily in our days.

I would like to thank all of my friends and family…..  Finally, I would like to thank everyone who came here today for honoring me with their presence.

--

[2/24/21, 11:22:29 AM] ‪+1 (310) 666‑2302‬: B”H

Dear Mrs. Bond,

Happy Purim!

The holiday of Purim is celebrated by sharing food gift baskets with friends and family, hearing the "Megillah"*, as well as dressing up in costume.

2000 years ago in Persia, there was a decree to annihilate the Jewish population. Through the bravery and heroism of Esther the Jewish woman hero, the Jewish people were saved.

The sages point out that Esther as queen would have been spared of this decree, nevertheless, she put herself at risk to save the nation.
Until today, we learn from Esther what it means to care for our greater community.

The above story may be more relevant now than ever before.
Over this seemingly endless pandemic, the need for deep communal connections and bonds is highlighted on a daily basis.

This Purim let's all try to emulate Queen Esther and find ways, no matter the circumstances to be there for another person, materially or spiritually.

Over the millennia we have always found a way to celebrate. This year won't be any different!

On behalf of Chabad of West Bel Air, please enjoy this Purim basket including the holidays festive foods and a Megillah to read the story of our shared heritage.

Purim is best celebrated with others. 

If you can't safely gather with friends or family, share a picture of your Purim box with them or connect via video.

Chag Sameach!

*If you would like a private and safe Megillah reading at your home for your family, 
please text or call 3106662302 by February 24.

Best wishes for a happy and healthy Purim,
Rabbi Mendy and Rebbitzen Dobie Mentz
Co-Directors Chabad of West Bel Air 

P.S. If there is any way we can be there for you or your family during these times, let us know and we will do our best to help!

פורים החל בערב שבת-  סדר פורס מפה ומקדש -מיוחד למקורבים המשתתפים בבית חב"ד(שאצל כו"כ מהם זו היא ההזדמנות לקיים מצות היום והתוועדות פורים).
1. להזמין הקהל בשיעור זמן מספיק לפני הדלקת נרות להספיק לקיים מצוות היום.
2. תפלת מנחה של ערב שבת.
3. קריאת המגילה. 
4. משלוח מנות ומתנות לאביונים. 
5. סעודת פורים בנטילת ידים והמוציא(עכ"פ כזית לחם *לפני* הדלק"נ), ובשר ויין.
6.הדלקת נרות בזמנה .
7. לאחר הדלק"נ יכין לחם משנה מכוסה במפה ויאמר קידוש של שבת על כוס יין (בכדי להתיר המשך סעודה אחרי השקיעה).
8. אם כבר בירך הגפן על יין בהתחלת הסעודה,יאמר רק ויכולו ואשר קדשנו, וידלג על ברכת הגפן.
9.יבצע הלחם משנה -בלי ברכת המוציא (שכבר ברכו בהתחלת הסעודה. ואם יש אחד שעדיין לא בירך המוציא יברך ויוציא הקהל  בברכה )- ויתן לכל אחד כזית  לאכול. 
10. ימשיך בסעודת שבת והתוועדות פורים  בשמחה , ונכון לאכול כזית חלה משחשיכה. ובברכת המזון יאמר על הניסים  ורצה. 
11. לאחר ברכת המזון מתפלל קבלת שבת ומעריב .
א פריילאכין פורים, מרדכי פרקש.

נ.ב. כמובן אם אפשר לערוך הסעודה ומצוות היום בשעות היום עדיף. אבל במצב שהקהל לא יגיע בשעות היום או שליח שעוסק במשך היום לזכות רבים במצוות היום -ינהג עם המקורבים כמבואר בזה.

Ultimately it comes down to what your style is, but one thing you can do which is kind of the best of both, is to post on your personal page, but tag your rebbetzin and also tag your chabad as the location. [3/3/21, 10:59:20 PM] ‪+1 (862) 812‑6224‬: Conversions to Judaism are only kosher when done according
to the rules of G-d Almighty.
Dear Fellow Shluchim,

I am sending out this email because I received personally a directive & blessing from the Rebbe on this issue. (exposing the Reform & Conservative movement for what they are --- NOT JEWISH)

The blessing and encouragement was handed to me by Rabbi L. Groner who while giving me the answer (credit to him for conveying the Rebbes answer to me) he told me, the Rebbe most likely did not read my package I submitted, and, if I took the Rebbes answer and directive to heart he would personally see to it that I became no more Shliach !!!! The following words I share with you, isn’t an easy task to carry out – Rabbi Groner as the secretary of the Rebbe failed, on this matter.  

Well, I have more faith in the answers of the Rebbe to specific questions asked, and even if my personal story is to be set aside, the Rebbe himself spent hundreds if not thousands of hours in public, in person, and in writing on this subject.

Now, I know this isn’t easy to stand up to. I live in the same world as everyone else, and I know pretty well, what, and who, we are dealing with.

When any of us signed up to be a Chabad Shliach, we signed up to Milchemes Bais Dovid. Tzivois Hashem Kipshuto -- The war of King David to eradicate the evil Amalek. The first thing Moshiach must succeed in accomplishing. 

Wars mean wounded and fatalities. It IS NOT all fun and games. But we go with the Rebbe as our commander in Chief. We are fighting G-ds war, like the Maccabees – “Who is to G-d, come to me”. The Rambam warns us, being afraid of this war, to fight, is literally a sin.

When someone has a cancer, it is not enough just the positive reinforcement, while there are aggressive tumors growing. Aggressive action is necessary to cut out the cancer and enemy to the person’s life, because no matter how much positive reinforcement, the cancer will win if the sickness is not eradicated.

The Rebbe fought for years, that the Conservative and Reform movements are NOT JEWISH movements. They do NOT represent the tradition of Moses and of G-d. The Rebbe fought for years, to change the wording back to its original phrase in the Law of Return in Israel – conversion “ACCORDING TO HALACHA”. 

What happened in Israel these last few days where the Supreme Court “in Israel” decided all conversions are equally acceptable is a DEATH BLOW to the very existence of our Jewish identity. (much worse even than what the Rebbe spoke before this last tragic turn of events at the Supreme Court in Israel.)

Chabad as a powerful voice in the Jewish world needs to come out with a STRONG PROCLAMATION against this Supreme Court Decision. (for the sake of our mission, for the sake of the Shluchim themselves, for the sake of our very own children). Anyone with a brain in his head, and a heart in his body, should shudder at what this court ruling will lead to, if left unopposed.

There is an evil virus killing the best of ours, it is maiming countless people who remain alive. Frum people seem to be disproportionately affected by the virus. G-d is waiting for a major effort on our part, to restore proper healthy equilibrium in the world.

It is up to the largest Jewish Organization in the world to take a very public stance on this matter. Staying quiet is a sin in itself. 

Chabad MUST come out in a unified fashion with a CLEAR proclamation -- The World expects this leadership -- the Rebbe expects it from his soldiers .

Conversions to Judaism are only kosher when done according to the rules of G-d Almighty. 

I am not including any sources in Halacha or the Rebbes works -- since they are literally countless.

[3/4/21, 4:06:35 PM] ‪+1 (516) 423‑6510‬: As shluchim, mental health is a subject that we encounter all too often. I was trained in Mental Health First Aid a in 2016 and it changed the way I think, deal and feel with those that are facing mental health conditions. I feel so strongly about it, I spent a week to be trained as a MHFA instructor in 2019. I gave a number of Mental Health First Aid trainings before the pandemic and recently started giving it online. Its an 8 hour course and its a commitment. The students both locally in person and online from all over the USA included shluchim that do not regret the time spent. Participants have access a great reference book to use as a reference. The Shluchim report how it  has helped them tremendously in their shlichus.

*A month ago we posted about opening up the MHFA course for virtual training online on this group and a few other groups and it was filled up in a few hours!* We were amazed at the response! Seeing the interest and in response to requests for more, we are happy to report that we just got further funding to offer more virtual trainings. *The grant that we currently have for free trainings ends April 30th. Chap Arein!*

*This time, we will be offering one exclusively for men participants and one exclusively for women participants.* Both trainings will be conducted by MHFA Certified National Instructors Rabbi Chaim Lazaroff and Mrs. Gittel Francis, both are shluchim in Houston.

Rabbi Chaim Lazaroff is the program director for Chabad Lubavitch of Texas and co-director of Chabad of Uptown / YJP Houston. Mrs Gittel Francis, LMSW is a Community Intervention Specialist for Jewish Family Service Houston.

Mental Health First Aid has nationwide appeal with over 2 million people trained. Huge corporations are taking this training on and mandating all their employees to be trained.  

You can read more about the program here  https://www.mentalhealthfirstaid.org.

Due to covid, the National Council for Behaviorial Health has pivoted to an online process for taking this course. The virtual delivery of the course has two components.
Part I:  Approximately 2 hours in length, pre-work on your own pace.
Part II: Approximately 6.5 hours in length (including breaks) and is co-lead virtually by MHFA Certified National Instructors 9 am-3:30 pm CST

Since it is all online anyone can join from anywhere. Upon completion of the training you will receive a certificate valid for three years. Limited spaces are available and early registration will afford you more time to get the pre-work done on your own pace. This is a $75 course, but thanks to a grant it is sponsored and FREE for you to take.
‍
*BOTH TRAININGS WILL BE HELD FROM 9AM-3:30 PM CST (Houston time)*

👉🏻 *MEN* MONDAY APRIL 26 https://bit.ly/3860Y7R

Dear {{First name}},

Thank you for your recent gift of {{amount}} to VC! Please accept this brief letter of thanks as my way of expressing gratitude for your kindness and generosity. :)

Purim is behind us! Passover is in sight!

There is a common theme that links both of these highly celebrated and enjoyed holidays: freedom.

The story line is not a new one. There was a threat and a struggle followed by triumph and victory!!

In the Purim story we were saved from complete annihilation. 

On Passover we were saved from the depths of literal slavery and the horrible state of slave mentality. 

Freedom!!!

We were born to be free! Free to be our best selves, free to share our unique gifts with the world!

Your gift to VC opens the path to freedom for teens to reach beyond themselves when volunteering with "special friends!"

Your investment with VC nurtures toddlers in their hands-on discovery of the beauty and joys of Yiddishkeit and Jewish tradition!

Some define freedom by what they are not forced to do.

Others create the tools for the generation following them, to explore, to give, to grow and
find meaning by living a life where they are free to enhance the people and the world around them.

Thank you for being a freedom igniter for the men, women, and children of all ages throughout the Pascack Valley and Saddle River communities! The world as we know it today is searching for light, comfort and stability. Also known as redemption :). 

Thank you for giving the gift of freedom!

My heartfelt thanks and best wishes,
Rabbi Dov

[3/8/21, 11:25:08 AM] Yaakov Koppel Chaiton: I am sorry to hear of the passing of your dear wife and mother. There are no adequate words to comfort one that has lost a parent, because regardless of age no one is ever ready to lose their guidance and love from a mother or spouse. May you experience only good things and plenty of happiness and joy from now on.

We have never actually met, so please allow me to briefly introduce myself. About 2 years ago, together with my wife and family we moved to the Hamilton—Robbinsville area to open up the first Jewish presence in this neighborhood. Over this period of time we have had the chance to meet many wonderful Jewish families. I look forward to getting to know you and I am only sorry this came up under such difficult circumstances.


If I may, allow me to offer a consoling thought at this difficult time.

We mere mortals cannot understand or fathom the ways of G-d, which sometimes leave us wondering. To be sure, believing in G-d as the creator and director of all is not in contradiction to crying out in protest of tragedy. On the contrary, complaining to G-d is a sign of our faith in his existence.

It is virtually impossible for human beings, with their limited capacity of intellect and emotion, to be able to deal with even the norms of day-to-day life, let alone something as tragic and unacceptable as the death of a loved one. For this G-d gave us His holy Torah containing His divine wisdom. Only G-d, the creator of life and death, can give us guidance through these challenges.

The Torah clearly states that only the physical body leaves us. The ‘Neshoma’ (soul) lives on forever and ever. Today we no longer have to take this on faith. Science has proven, that an energy that existed once continues to exist forever! Be assured that the soul of your beloved wife and mother will continue to live on, as she looks down upon her beloved children and family. She will rejoice in your happiness and be a part of your daily lives and challenges.

We, as Jews have never been limited to the realm of the physical. Our strength and ability to retain ourselves as a people throughout the millennia of persecution has been, and always will be, the dominant strength of our spirit. This is true with us as a people. It is also true with each and every one of us as an individual.


I hope these teachings of our holy Torah offer some consolation in this great loss. May G-d bless you with his warmth and compassion so that you no longer know of any sorrow, and may he give you the strength to persevere and overcome this terrible loss and enable you to carry on in your life, a life so productive, fulfilling and meaningful, with plenty of Nachat. And you should be blessed with a New Year full of only good things.
Sincerely,

Rabbi Yaakov Chaiton

[3/9/21, 4:47:12 PM] ‪+61 450 095 828‬: That you can't compare pain. The pain of this happening to such a person vs the pain someone else experiences from something else?

Eg, the pain of loosing your wallet vs the pain of your favourite ice cream flavour not being in the shop today...

To the person experiencing the ice cream pain, his pain is not necessarily less than the guy who list his wallet. 

Cuz pain is experienced subjectively.
[3/9/21, 4:47:39 PM] ‪+1 (510) 640‑2590‬: Oh
[3/9/21, 4:50:44 PM] ‪+61 450 095 828‬: Another example.

The same painful experience happening to 2 different people who live in different circumstances.

Eg 
A poor and homeless person being/feeling bullied 
Vs
Meghan Merkel being/feeling bullied

There's no hierarchy to pain here would say that Merkel's pain is not any "less painful" than the poor person.
[3/9/21, 4:53:47 PM] ‪+61 450 095 828‬: Maybe you can see this idea expressed in the Mitzvah of Tzedoko.

Where we don't set a threshold. But rather, for example in a case of a rich person going broke, the Torah doesn't set an objective approach to providing him food and shelter, but *rather* takes into account his *subjective* "pain" and therefore tells us to sustain him in a fitting way as a "Gvir" ie provide to him what he is used to.

As in the past, Chabad.org will feature every proclamation they receive on dedicated page on their website. This includes, states, counties, cities, townships - you name it. If it says Education and Sharing Day on it, it will IYH go up.

In order for your proclamation to be up there, you need to do these 2 easy steps.

1. Have a high resolution PDF of the proclamation.

2. Send it to educationday5781@gmail.com with the name of the state/city/county etc.

That's it!

The earlier you send it, the earlier it gets posted.

Thank you to all the wonderful chassidim at Chabad.org for taking care of this!

[3/25/21, 8:18:52 AM] Chaim Markovits Chaim Hillel: [Adai Ad - Just One Thing]
*EXPECT THAT SOMETHING WILL GO AWRY.*

Inevitably, something will go awry.  Someone will say something you (and they) wish they hadn’t. Schedules will get off track. Something will happen with some food. There’ll be something. Even with the best planning.

There is no such thing as perfection. Not for one day and certainly not over the whole yom tov. *Expect that something will happen. You’ll be less frustrated and disappointed when it does.  And if nothing actually happens, then you’ll be pleasantly surprised.*

Dear Mr. & Mrs. Smith:

Thank you for your recent contribution to Chabad of NW Metro Denver of four hundred dollars. Your contribution will continue to help further a vibrant Jewish identity and awareness throughout our community.
This past Passover we reached hundrends of community members, with special handbaked matzah and complete Seder Packages of matzah, wine/grape juice and a delicious holiday meal that we deliverd to home-bound seniors and nursing home residents as part of the Seder Project. (see enclosed flyer).
In addittion, we hosted two community seders with limited particpants to comply with Covid guidelines.
Please know that as a result of your partnership with Chabad of NW Metro Denver, the words of the Hagadah “whoever is hungry let them come and eat” were fulfilled, with many community members enjoying Passover food of both physical and spiritual nourishment.

In merit of your genoristy may you and yours be granted the blessings of good health, happiness and prosperity.

With warm regards,
[4/13/21, 8:20:31 AM] Chaim Markovits Chaim Hillel: On behalf of the Chabad Center of Sudbury I would like to express my thanks and appreciation for your generous contribution/s towards the work of the center.  During these challenging times when so much has changed and many are dealing with personal hardship, your kind support has helped make a real difference to our efforts at providing support, meaning and inspiration to so many. 

In recent months with the support of people like yourself we were able to hand deliver joy to many hundreds of homes in the greater Sudbury area. This included over three hundred Purim packages that were hand delivered before the holiday and helped bring an added dose of joy to the holiday. Likewise for Passover we delivered almost two hundred and fifty Passover care packages that were hand delivered with some extra care and a personal touch and sixty Passover Catered Dinners that were brought to the homes of homebound seniors or others who it made a difference to.

In the words of one recipient, “as a senior living alone, I had no way to have a Seder this year, until your thoughtful and beautiful Passover Seder Dinner was brought to my door, and enabled me to celebrate the joy of this holiday”.

In addition, in recent months we have continued to hold many socially distant programs and services for children, adults and families, as well as a wide range of Adult Ed activities via Zoom.

Thank G-d, the tide is beginning to turn against the Pandemic and more and more people are getting vaccinated and the future looks brighter and more hopeful. At the same time, we say thank you to you for being a part of these efforts to make the world brighter and more connected, even during the challenges of the last few months. It is our prayer and wish, that we collectively overcome the current challenges and come out stronger and better in a brighter and improved world. 

In closing, I extend my wishes to you and your family that you continue to see success in all of your endeavors coupled with good health, joy and prosperity.

Sincerely yours,

Rabbi Yisroel Freeman 
Director

P.S. This letter serves as proof of receipt for your tax-deductible donation.  Please keep it for your tax records.  Donor did not receive any material goods or services.

Todah is Hebrew for thank you. 

It’s actually much more than thank you. It speaks of gratitude, appreciation, thanks and praise.  Lots of beauty packed into one word. 

Todah for your recent gift of {{amount}} to Valley Chabad. 

The world is in Spring mode. More sunshine, new budding flowers, warmer weather and the feeling of rebirth. 

On the Jewish calendar, we are in the days of Sefirat Haomer. A time for self work, reflection, and personal growth. The Omer is counted in preparation for receiving the Torah on the upcoming Shavuos holiday.

Your generosity is sparking joy and life with the seniors in the community! Your commitment to Jewish life is the greatest gesture in support of Torah lessons and values!

Thank you for being a key partner in the rebirth of life and happiness at Valley Chabad. 

My best wishes for a healthy summer and lots of fresh air, in good company and in the best of health!!!

Rabbi Dov

A Texan is visiting Israel and feeling thirsty, he stops at a house along the road. "Can you give me a drink?" asks the Texan

"What do you do?" asks the Texan.

"Well," says the Texan, "on my ranch, I have breakfast and get into the car, and I drive and drive and I don't reach the end of the ranch until dinnertime."

[4/21/21, 5:25:14 PM] ‪+1 (716) 650‑0613‬: It's about being sensitive

They say a story about a shliach that a mekurov walked into chabad and wanted to say kaddish for his dog. 

The shliach told him that it would be a great thing, just we need to be certain that dog was jewish? 

The mekurov said he is certain that the dog was jewish, since he ate matzah balls every shabbos and matzah on pesach etc.

The shliach agreed but said 'How do we know the dogs mother was jewish'?

To this the mekurov had no answer. The Shliach told him to wait a few minutes, and he will figure something out.

A few minutes later the shliach returned smiling: It's a sofek if the dog's mother was jewish, casting doubt about the deceased dog. Because of this sofek, you can't say kaddish for the dog. 

However in Hazlocha there is a Klal that shomya k'one, so if someone else says kaddish, and you answer Amen, it's as if you said kaddish yourself.

Therefore you should come three times daily to shul and answer amen to someone else's kaddish and it's as if you yourself said kaddish.

A year later this mekurov was frum...

The shliach could have easily mocked the mekurov etc.

L'chaim

[4/22/21, 10:16:44 PM] ‪+1 (917) 445‑1973‬: When a train filled with a large transport of Jewish prisoners arrived at one of the Nazi killing centers, many Polish gentiles came out to watch the latest group as they were taken away. As the disoriented Jews were gathering their possessions to take with them into the camp, a Nazi officer in charge called out to the villagers standing nearby, "Anything these Jews leave behind you may take for yourselves, because for sure they will not be coming back to collect them!"

Two Polish women who were standing nearby saw a woman towards the back of the group, wearing a large, heavy, expensive coat. Not waiting for someone else to take the coat before them, they ran to the Jewish woman and knocked her to the ground, grabbed her coat and scurried away.
Moving out of sight of the others, they quickly laid the coat down on the ground to divide the spoils of what was hiding inside. Rummaging through the pockets, they giddily discovered gold jewelry, silver candlesticks and other heirlooms. They were thrilled with their find, but as they lifted the coat again, it still seemed heavier than it should. Upon further inspection, they found a secret pocket, and hidden inside the coat was .... a tiny baby girl!

Shocked at their discovery, one woman took pity and insisted to the other, "I don't have any children, and I'm too old to give birth now. You take the gold and silver and let me have the baby." The Polish woman took her new "daughter" home to her delighted husband. They raised the Jewish girl as their own, treating her very well, but never telling her anything about her history. The girl excelled in her studies and even became a doctor, working as a pediatrician in a hospital in Poland.

When her "mother" passed away many years later, a visitor came to pay her respects. An old woman invited herself in and said to the daughter, "I want you to know that the woman that passed away last week was not your real mother ..." and she proceeded to tell her the whole story. She did not believe her at first, but the old woman insisted.

"When we found you, you were wearing a beautiful gold pendant with strange writing on it, which must be Hebrew.
I am sure that your mother kept the necklace. Go and see for yourself." Indeed, the woman went into her deceased mother's jewelry box and found the necklace just as the elderly lady had described. She was shocked. It was hard to fathom that she had been of Jewish descent, but the proof was right there in her hand. As this was her only link to a previous life, she cherished the necklace. She had it enlarged to fit her neck and wore it every day, although she thought nothing more of her Jewish roots.

Some time later, she went on holiday abroad and came across two Jewish boys standing on a main street, trying to interest Jewish passersby to wrap Tefillin on their arms (for males) or accept Shabbos candles to light on Friday afternoon (for females). Seizing the opportunity, she told them her entire story and showed them the necklace. The boys confirmed that a Jewish name was inscribed on the necklace but did not know about her status. They recommended that she write a letter to their mentor, the Lubavitcher Rebbe, explaining everything. If anyone would know what to do, it would be him.

She took their advice and sent off a letter that very same day. She received a speedy reply saying that it is clear from the facts that she is a Jewish girl and perhaps she would consider using her medical skills in Israel where talented pediatricians were needed. Her curiosity was piqued and she traveled to Israel where she consulted a Rabbinical Court (Beit Din) who declared her Jewish. Soon she was accepted into a hospital to work, and eventually met her husband and raised a family.

In August 2001, a terrorist blew up the Sbarro cafe in the center of Jerusalem. The injured were rushed to the hospital where this woman worked. One patient was brought in, an elderly man in a state of shock. He was searching everywhere for his granddaughter who had become separated from him.
Asking how she could recognize her, the frantic grandfather gave a description of a gold necklace that she was wearing.

Eventually, they finally found her among the injured patients.
At the sight of this necklace, the pediatrician froze. She turned to the old man and said, "Where did you buy this necklace?"
"You can't buy such a necklace," he responded, "I am a goldsmith and I made this necklace. Actually I made two identical pieces for each of my daughters. This is my granddaughter from one of them, and my other daughter did not survive the war."

And this is the story of how a Jewish girl, brutally torn away from her mother on a Nazi camp platform almost sixty years ago, was reunited with her father .....

Adapted from the book "Heroes of Faith"

[4/26/21, 12:15:13 PM] ‪+1 (718) 913‑8336‬: For those that didn’t see Nosson’s message on the Covid relief group, will post it here:

Based on two conversations I had today, I was moved to write the following about the expanded EIDL loans.  It’s long, and it’s not strictly financial tips.  Feel free to skip this one.

What we're seeing here is really unprecedented.  A loan for amazing terms, for an amount equaling two times our annual budget, up to $500K.    All this at a time when, as far as I can tell,  many/most US Shluchim actually did well, financially, in the last 12 months; relatively few are currently experiencing a financial crisis.

As Shluchim, our first (and only!) responsibility is how to fulfill our Shlichus.  What does the Rebbe teach us about this? Ask your own mashpiah/head Shliach/whomever.  The following are just my thoughts:

First point: Grab the opportunity!

Everything starts and finishes with עמך ישראל, and as per תניא פרק ב' and numerous references in chassidus and the Rebbe's writings,  כל ההשפעות עוברות דרך נשיא הדור.   In simple terms: It’s not Biden or Trump. It’s the Rebbe showering us with ברכות.  And he has always been very clear about our responsibility to every single נשמה in our respective communities.     Who gave us the right NOT to take advantage of what's offered to us, and bring our mosdos and activities to an entirely new level?!

Of course, everything must be done in  כלים דתיקון ... But at the same time, we all have big תוהו projects we always wanted to do but thought we simply couldn't afford.  Take the money, run and do it!  You don't have such a project? Ask your mashpiah/head Shliach/coach/whomever for ideas.   But when an opportunity knocks on our door, we should at least *consider* grabbing it!  

Here's one reminder:  There are hundreds of couples looking for a Shlichus, and there are many souls in your community whom you didn’t reach.   Not every place can use more help ...but many can, and today, you can't really claim that start-up money is your problem.

But then there is the second, counter-point:   כלים דתיקון!

It’s doubly important to be responsible with "the Rebbe's" money.  I can think of many foolish ways to blow money ... and have seen so many young guys drown in CC debt.

1.	Don’t borrow anything to maintain your regular budget.  That’s what fundraising is for.  Use this for special project(s), and stick to it!
2.	If you have/had a debt-management problem … borrowing is probably still a bad idea.
3.	Whatever you have in mind, discuss it with someone on the outside to for a reality & כלים דתיקון  check.
4.	If a project is launched with 100% borrowed funds, i.e. there no “real” support for it, it’s quite possibly a bad idea.
5.	The money does eventually have to be paid back.  We aren’t “businesses”, but it’s probably OK to borrow the business term of “good debt” vs. “bad debt”.  “Good debt” is an investment which will make it financially worthwhile long-term.

And then there is point three, which can't be emphasized enough:  

**everything MUST be 1000% legal and above board**.

Money is flowing today, but in classic American tradition, I expect there to be prosecutions related to this program for many years to come.   

For one: Remember to maintain a clear distinction between your mosad and your personal life.    In your mind, you may be morally justified taking $200K and using it as a down-payment to buy a home or renovate an existing one (“for the benefit of the mosad!”); paying down your mortgage; marrying off several of your children; or simply catching up on several years worth of deferred salary.  **All of these are real questions I got just  in the last few days**

Remember: Even in regular times, whenever a mosad does these types of things it has to be done properly.  By default, if a large amount of $ suddenly goes to your pocket it isn’t proper!

Many things could be kosher if once you create the proper agreements and board resolutions, and maintain the proper records. But in the case of this EIDL loan, there are more restrictions about the use of the funds – and this time, they’ll be watching!    It’s doubly important that these funds are used for the Mosad’s purposes and not your own.  It may still be possible to work it all out; but  whatever you do, please, work with a professional and make sure you're 1000% above board.  

To a somewhat lesser degree, the same is true even for Chabad projects.  The official rules do not allow these funds to be used for capital campaigns, or to pay down your existing mortgage.    Over time and with proper records, it appears one can accomplish these goals properly and legally – but again, spend the time and work with a financial expert to make sure you’re good.  It’s worth every dime!

(Don’t ask me for names – I don’t have any recommendations).

***

All this is just my own opinion.   I expect many to disagree with some of these points, especially the first premise which many will feel is irresponsible.  The Rebbe wanted each of us to have who to ask these questions.   You owed it to the Rebbe to go and ask whoever your authority is.

[4/28/21, 8:13:52 PM] ‪+52 612 348 8808‬: HTWSSTKS is an acronym with connections to the Masonic Temple, specifically Royal Arch Masons. The letters stand for, “Hiram, Tyrian, Widow’s Son, Sent to King Solomon.” Of course, now we’re left wondering who the heck Hiram is!

As it turns out, all third degree Freemasons study the story of a man named Hiram Abiff (a.k.a. Hiram the Widow’s Son.) According to legend, Hiram was chief architect for the Temple of King Solomon. When bad guys tried to squeeze the secret masonic passwords out of Hiram, he valiantly refused to tell them. As a result, the bad guys killed poor Hiram. In Masonic teachings, Hiram’s story is held up as an example of loyalty.

So, when you see HTWWTKS on someone’s headstone, you know that not only were they a Royal Arch Mason, but that they made it at least as far as the third degree in that fraternal order!

[4/29/21, 9:42:50 PM] ‪+1 (928) 600‑6331‬: My heart is torn open.

As the festival of Lag B'Omer, a joyous celebration of unity and love of one's fellow Jew began in Israel earlier today, a tragic accident occured. 

While reports are still coming in, it seems evident that the worst has happened, and there are multiple deaths, and catastrophic injuries R"L. 

When I had the privilege to live in the the Holy Land, I would often walk the valley from my Yeshiva in Tzfas to the mountain of Meron, to pray at the resting place of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the compiler of the Zohar, and a hero of Jewish continuity. 

A highlight each year was Lag B'Omer, when hundreds of thousands of Jews would join together in Meron, at his resting place, and celebrate his legacy.

The joy of Lag B'Omer in Meron is indescribable, as bonfires rage, and Jews of every background celebrate together, as one people. Every person who comes to the Rashbi is family.

As I watch the reports of the devastating news, I see the pain of my family. I see the catastrophic pain caused to those hurt, and to the families of those who lost their lives.

Lag B'Omer comes between Passover and Shavuos, a period we refer to as the Omer. During this period, we mourn the loss of the students of Rabbi Akiva who passed away in a tragic plague. Our 
mourning only ceases on Lag B'Omer, when we celebrate the life of Rabbi 
Shimon, a surviving student of Rabbi Akiva, who taught that loving your fellow Jew is an essential principle of Judaism. 

Today however, that joy is marred by the pain we feel for and with our brothers and sisters. 

Lag B'Omer is celebrating with festive bonfires, yet tonight, essential lights were snuffed out. 

Tomorrow, as Lag B'Omer concludes, Shabbos will begin. Before it does, my wife will light a fire of her own, to beckon in the Shabbos, and the peace and tranquility that accompany it. 

This week, in honor of Lag B'Omer, and in memory of those holy sparks removed from our world, I ask you to join her. 

Where ever you are in the world, light a candle as Shabbos comes in, and bring much needed illumination into the world. The time in Lexington is 8:10 pm.

May God bring a speedy recovery to all those in need, and may He comfort the families among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem.

Ad Mosai!
