[4/30/21, 2:51:33 PM] ‪+52 612 348 8808‬: If needed

BS"D  In regards to the unspeakable  tragedy: Tens of thousands of people will have witnessed this event on the internet as it was streamed live, or via photos and videos on social media and the news.

There will be those who may become emotionally upset by simply learning about the event from friends, without any exposure to photos of the disaster scene.

Below is a short list of eight fundamental ideas about coping with disaster that you may find helpful if you feel affected by this event- in addition to praying for the welfare of the injured and seeing if there is any other practical help you are able to provide.

One, it is normal to feel traumatized or affected emotionally and psychologically by this type of event. People react in all sorts of ways to traumatic incidents. You may have trouble sleeping, feel sad, have intrusive thoughts, a lack of appetite, or other symptoms of trauma in lieu of the Meron Disaster.

Experts reassure that it is quite normal and even expected to have symptoms like these immediately after such an event. It has been described as a "normal reaction to abnormal circumstances". This is how our bodies and minds react to such unthinkable tragedies. Do not panic or be overly concerned if this happens to you.

You are not alone in having such feelings.

Two, you are permitted to feel sad or shocked about this event even if you did not personally lose somebody in this incident. Some trauma incidents occur on such a large scale that we, as the Jewish people, feel emotionally connected to what happened regardless of having any direct personal involvement.

You did not need to have travelled to Meron this year to feel sad or affected by this event. You do not need to feel stupid or guilty that you feel anything at all concerning this event. You do not need to feel guilty that you feel indifferent or empty if this is what you feel. You are permitted to feel exactly as you do right now, and this is acceptable.

You are not alone in having such feelings.

Three, some people may feel guilty that they were not harmed in this disaster while others were injured or killed. Thoughts like "why did I survive while they didn't?" can come up in our minds and feel challenging.

These types of thoughts commonly occur after escaping such incidents without harm and this phenomenon is well known.

If this happens to you, you are not alone in having such thoughts.

Four, after events like these it is common to ask oneself or other people questions such as "why did this happen?" or "why on Lag Ba'Omer, on such a joyous day and holy site?"

It is okay to have such questions. You may or may not find answers to them now or ever. In fact, you may not even be seeking an answer but a way to express shock and surprise by talking about this event in the form of a question. This is common and okay.

If you feel like you are carrying around questions like these and feeling shocked, you are not alone.


Five, if you are feeling some challenging emotions or reacting in some way to the tragic event, you can think of some practical ways to cope.

I invite you to pause and think of a safe reasonable way of coping that might help you. Can you think of something which would make you feel calmer, better, or at ease?

Here are some time-tested coping methods that you might find helpful. Feel free to try them as needed-

-Call a trusted friend and share with them whatever you feel you want to. Get a hug. Be listened to. Reach out to people who you feel could hear your feelings or story.

-Go for a walk around the block or neighborhood by yourself or with a friend.

-Listen to calming music.

-Reduce your exposure to media coverage of the disaster.

-Talk to a professional.

-Avoid using alcohol and drugs as a method of coping with challenging thoughts or feelings. There are many reasons for this.

There are many ways to cope with trauma. Discover the ways that help you feel more at ease. See what you can come up with. If you would like, consult with a trusted friend or professional on how to do this.

Six, Take it easy. These types of events have a major impact on our bodies and minds. They can be overwhelming, tiring, depressing, or confusing. Make sure to eat, drink, rest, and take it easy as needed. Sometimes we need to slow down and take care of ourselves, and that is okay.

Seven, Difficult thoughts and feelings from such disasters usually begin to subside after a few days from when the incident occurred. For others, these symptoms may persist for a few weeks and then go away. For a smaller group of people, these symptoms may persist for a month and even longer. You are invited to consult with a professional at any time for assistance.

If you find yourself having a challenging time after 3 days from the incident has passed, experts recommend that you connect with a trusted professional to get some assistance.

If you find yourself having thoughts of suicide you should seek assistance immediately.

Over the next few days, I hope that we will see a slew of services available for those seeking counseling and emotional support in light of these tragic events.

Here are two resources available right now-

"Eran" operates an emotional support hotline which can be reached by dialing 1201. Dial the number without a star before or after it.

For people seeking help specifically from clinicians sensitive to religious people, the Bayit Cham organization is running a special hotline which can be reached by dialing *9518.

Eight, If you know somebody who appears traumatized by the disaster, consider approaching that person and asking if they would like to talk. If they express interest, try to give them an opportunity to share with you whatever they want to. Listen to them nonjudgmentally and with empathy. Do not ask them to tell you their story if they do not offer to.

Ask directly if there is anything they would like from you at this time. If their request is reasonable, see if you can help them with it. Encourage them to connect with a professional if you or they suspect that this is necessary. If you chat together and they express interest in learning ways to cope with traumatic stress, see if you can both together come up with some coping techniques that the person things will be helpful to them. Make sure that the person gets the support that they need.

Avi Tenenbaum is an expert in Disaster Behavioral Health and Psychological First Aid. His experience includes providing aid for families coping in the wake of large-scale disasters and war including the Second Lebanon War, Hurricane Harvey, The Pittsburg Tree-of-Life massacre, the Haifa 2016 Fires, Operation Cast-Lead, Sorotzkin Arson Fires, and more. He can be reached at avitenenbaum9@gmail.com

Top takeaways from the new Pew study: Chabad, Israel, Jewish food and more

 Chabad draws a diverse — but limited — following of American Jews

For the first time in its surveys of Jews, Pew asked about Chabad, the Orthodox movement that offers Jewish programming across the United States. Researchers found that 16% of American Jews participate in Chabad’s activities “often” or “sometimes,” including services. But of those who participate “often” or “sometimes,” 27% are Reform, 26% are Conservative and 16% are unaffiliated. Another 21% of U.S. Jews said they “rarely” attended Chabad activities, for a total of 37% who have participated in some kind of Chabad programming at least once.

The ignorance about the I-P conflict is stunning and while death on any side is appalling, the moral equivalence argument is just nauseating.

However, some people who make these arguments are well-meaning and are just trying to support the “underdog”.  But what they’re actually doing is; emboldening terrorism, supporting murder, and condoning antisemitism.

So here are a few facts.

1. Did you know that there are 1.8 Billion Muslims and about 50 Muslim countries? There are only 14 million Jews and 1 Jewish country!

2. More than 6 Million Jews (1/3 of the entire Jewish population) were murdered in the 20th century. To protect the Jews from being slaughtered wholesale again, the UN and other world institutions gave the Jews this tiny country in the middle east called Israel, approximately the size of New Jersey. The goal? so Jews can live peacefully and protect themselves- because no else will protect them. (We won’t even talk about the fact that Jews have lived there for thousands of years…owned land, archeology etc...)

From the moment they became a state, their neighbors vowed to “push them into the sea”. Every few months they have a different excuse to try and murder as many Jews as possible.  
Intifadas, suicide bombings, incendiary balloons, rockets and more. Most recently, Abbas is about to lose his power (16 year term) to Hamas and needs a distraction, so here come the rockets. 

3. Did you know that Hamas just launched more than a thousand rockets at Israel? They shot these rockets towards civilians! Towards innocent civilians! Why would they do that?! Their goal is clear: murder as many Jews as possible. They say so themselves. Their leader just said the other day “buy a knife and decapitate a Jew, a knife is only 5 Shekels”

4. So in response to this terror, the IDF (Israel Defense Forces) being a highly moral army, makes “very targeted” strikes to remove these terrorists who are murdering people. Israel makes targeted strikes because they don’t want to kill anyone unnecessarily. Yes, Israel even drops leaflets, warning the civilians to get out from the Hamas launch pads. Isn't it strange that the Hamas launch pads are almost always situated in hospitals, schools and residential buildings? But somehow, Israel is labeled as the aggressor and the human rights violator?

5. Let’s stop for a moment and think. If Israel were to do what Hamas is doing, which is "use all your military might to murder civilians", then Israel has the military might to kill literally everyone in that region. But they would never do that or even think that because Israel has high morals and Israel values life. Not like the terrorists. 

6. Did you know That NO Jews are allowed in the Palestinian Territories? If you go there, you risk your life. Literally. When I was in Israel in 2019, there were huge red signs that the Israeli government installed that says “Israelis don’t go here, we can’t protect you.” When Jews do enter, they often don’t leave. But when a Palestinian enters Israel, what happens? they can get a cup of coffee and a croissant and go home.

7. These Palestinian areas are called “Juden Rein”. Remember that term from your history class?

Dear ______, 

Preparations are under way for the annual printing of the Jewish Art Calendar in Raleigh. The Jewish Life Center - Chabad will once again be producing this attractive multi-color publication and mailing it to  over 4,700 Jewish homes & local businesses in Raleigh and the surrounding areas free of charge.

The calendar will include detailed information about upcoming holidays, educational messages, Shabbat and Holiday candle lighting times, traditional Jewish recipes, and popular thematic artwork. The practical design also provides ample room for the recording of personal information and appointments. The calendar will also include many of the much-anticipated events and programs of Jewish Life Center - Chabad.

*New this year!* The calendar will also feature opportunities for your family's special occasions, e.g. Bar/Bat Mitzvah, Yahrzeits, birthdays and anniversaries, to be printed in the calendar.

To take advantage of this opportunity and to honor yourselves or a loved one with a mention in the calendar, please click here or visit www.jewishraleigh.org/advertise.

We believe this is also an extraordinary sponsorship opportunity to market your business or services to the Jewish community.  Unlike newspaper ads that are seen once and discarded, this business promotion will benefit you continuously, as it is displayed in homes and offices throughout the community the whole year round, thus ensuring optimum visibility for your products or services, and maximum return for your dollar. 

Your participation helps us with this worthy endeavor, as well as with our other efforts on behalf of Jewish continuity. Please take a moment to fill out the form online or print out this form and return it to us. Your early response will be greatly appreciated.

Warm regards,

[5/26/21, 10:10:46 PM] ‪+1 (330) 861‑8770‬: *28 Sivan - 80 years - Meeting Recap*

* 2 elements: 1) Huge miracle of the rescue of the Rebbe and Rebbetzin, 2) the "tnufah chadashah" in hafatzas hamayanos
* In 5749, following 3 years of 28 Sivan being celebrated, the Rebbe mentioned that 28 Sivan has already been established as a day....by ״רבים מישראל״
* There are very few days in Dor Hashvii that the Rebbe recognized that were "established" as special days... 5 Teves and 28 Sivan

*Practically:* Communities are encouraged to make a communal gathering/farbrengen event on 28 Sivan to mark and celebrate the day as well as a community-wide learning shabbos before on one of the mamorim or sichos of 28 Sivan.

The following are some of the resources available on www.celebration80.com

▫️Derher Magazine 
▫️School Curriculum 
▫️Flyer for a farbrengen and help to find a farbrengener for your community 
▫️You can order kovetz 28 Sivan
▫️Social media pictures and videos
▫️JEM videos
▫️Farbrengen by the Ohel and Central zoom

More information and links to each of the above can be found on www.celebration80.com

Chabad draws a diverse — but limited — following of American Jews

For the first time in its surveys of Jews, Pew asked about Chabad, the Orthodox movement that offers Jewish programming across the United States. Researchers found that 16% of American Jews participate in Chabad’s activities “often” or “sometimes,” including services. But of those who participate “often” or “sometimes,” 27% are Reform, 26% are Conservative and 16% are unaffiliated. Another 21% of U.S. Jews said they “rarely” attended Chabad activities, for a total of 37% who have participated in some kind of Chabad programming at least once.

[5/31/21, 11:22:17 AM] Menachem Orenstein: *Cookie Revenge and Flavor Chords*

In 1987 an anonymous letter started appearing in mailboxes all across the country, claiming to reveal the secret recipe to Mrs. Fields brand chocolate chip cookies.

The story it told was from an irate customer who bought the recipe for $2.50 only to find out that they charged her $250.00 on her card. So to take revenge, they are sending the recipie to everyone across the country.

(it took money and effort to send out Spam in those days).

The recipe turned out to be bogus. But it did spark something for young Todd Wilbur.

It got him thinking...what is this secret recipe that everyone’s talking about?

So he transformed his kitchen into a makeshift science lab. And he then baked thousand of cookies. He compared each batch to the genuine Mrs. Fields cookies. He took detailed notes, video and audio recordings, and tweaked each iteration until he was satisfied that he broke the code.

But he didn’t stop there. He was hooked on “decoding” food. And he went on to decode various famous popular food (which you have never tasted).

Why did this become such a passion of his? 

If he wanted to eat that food, let him just buy it?

The reason is, he didn’t want that food to eat. He wanted to understand that food so he can see what ingredients work well with others.

He called them Flavor Chords.

Here’s an example of a Flavor Chord. 

Basil + Mozzarella + Tomato

Garlic + ginger + soy

By understanding how these ingredients work together, he could use them in other applications.

He could make different and unfamiliar food taste good to you by evoking those same flavor chords.

And this brings us to today’s lesson.

There is a recipe in fundraising.

Gift + gratitude + meaningful difference + attention = Happy Donors

Happy Donors = Repeat donors

You can solve almost any fundraising problem with this formula. (I did it yesterday on the 2020 group.)

But you need to know more than just the names of ingredients. You need to see it in action. You need to see how it is presented. You need to see how an experienced chef does it.

And we have a special opportunity that starts next week. We have 10 different chefs show us how to express gratitude, show appreciation, show the donors the difference they make, how to give them attention.

It’s not about copying other people. 

You’ll learn new fundraising chords to build your own masterpiece.

95 Shluchim have already joined. They’ll be tuning in from most states, coast to coast. As well as from Canada, Mexico, Luxembourg, France, England, South Africa, Australia,

I’m sure I’m missing some countries.

If you haven’t joined already, it’s not too late. www.growgelt.com

If you need a discount, please let me know - we have some subsidies available.

[5/31/21, 7:18:54 PM] ‪+1 (718) 913‑8336‬: No one is forcing anyone to use a coach. 

Coaches time is also valuable. Some of them have other (busy) jobs, it has to be worth their time. (Similarly to a Shliach charging a plant $1,500 to go give a hechsher).

The good coaches also work for you and are available even when they are “not on the clock”.

Additionally, Coaches are mugbal in time, one of the ways to make sure they are working with someone committed is to charge a proper fee. (There is a story, I believe with Rabbi Mordechai Rivkin, that the Rebbe told him to HIRE a chavrusah for learning this way he will take it more seriously).

In short, if you do not think it’s worth the cost there is no need to use it. 

How much the coach makes shouldn’t be your concern, it should be the value you are receiving. (No one argues with their lawyer over pricing, either you think it’s a fair value or you get another lawyer).

With all that said, I have never been able to pull the trigger on a coach, even though I would probably benefit tremendously.

[6/1/21, 12:16:51 AM] ‪+1 (617) 388‑6641‬: Fundraising is a serious skill. 
People spend years learning and "perfecting" the skill. 
Some people have an easier time asking people for money. Some have a very hard time making asks.
 
If it's easy for you to make asks, that's great. But there is still the knowledge of relationship building, cultivating, when, how and how much to ask, as well as stewardship. 
They are all important for successful fundraising. 

The bigger challenge is the fear of asking. I would venture to say this is a common challenge, much more common than we assume (ask around. There are veteran shluchim of many years who very seldomly make asks of new potential donors. 
Cultivating relationships that result in gifts coming in without asks is great. But if that's where most (all) of the funding is coming from it can be very dangerous. 
This is something that I personally deal with. 
I have had coaches for multiple years. 
They have helped me tremendously (technique, preparation, getting over fears, as well as accountability are huge) . I have spent lots of money on coaches and fundraising programs but the results make those sums pretty insignificant. 
I am responsible for my moised (and family). And I'll do whatever it takes to work on myself to make the fundraising happen. 
I'm doing Elazars grow gelt program next week. 
I raise money. But I'd like to raise more and do it more efficiently and professionally. 
I don't want to live in the "it's working for now" mode. I want to do my shlichus which includes fundraising to the best of my abilities.

"One thing that I'm taking, that I think we all could really learn from

She never said anything that wasn't kind or nice about anyone

And we had a fair share of weird and wonderful people to talk about

This one's dog, this one's funny lisp, this one's obsessions with pens, this one's stupid fight with his siblings etc

As kids we'd talk about it between ourselves, but she never ever said anything like that.

There was no rolling her eyes when she saw a weirdo coming towards the event

There was no complaining about the 'helpful people' who stayed to clean up

She was only kind and caring

I heard a story of a child of a shliach who didn't want to go to sleep on time Friday night, he said he wanted to stay up until after the meal "when we speak about the guests"

And to a certain degree I think many of us do that

At least I know I do

And I don't want that to be my kids

I don't want that to be me

I want to be like my mother

Who saw every opportunity to help a yid do a Mitzvah as a golden opportunity

And only saw their pure neshama"

[6/3/21, 5:31:17 PM] ‪+1 (425) 652‑8286‬: *Are you organized? Or are you...?*

Tayereh fellow Shliach,

Do you put together top quality Shiurim weekly, outlining your broad knowledge of the Rebbe’s Torah in beautifully designed source sheets - a week
in advance?

Do you prepare interesting sermons every week, weaving together topical stimulating ideas as a springboard of the lessons we find at the Makor of the Maayon - by Tuesday?

Do you have new catchy flyers with cutting edge graphic design - ready for every Yom Tov a few weeks before?

If your answer to the above questions is yes, please don’t read further and just go to www.togetherforshluchim.com and think about the rest of us. 

But if your answer is, like mine, a resounding no, then I hope you’re availing yourself to the lifesaving resources of The Shluchim Office.

The weekly Shiurim at www.jewishinsights.org

The weekly sermons at www.shluchimsermons.org

The constantly updated flyers at www.shluchim.org/flyers

(And the great Whatsapp support groups for each of these resources to get it all in real time). 

AND ALL AT NO COST FOR YOU AND ME!

So today is our chance 1. to say thank you and 2. To make sure that these and the literally dozens of other services that they provide for us all can continue at www.togetherforshluchim.com. 

Make a difference now!

Thank you for joining,

Oshy

They felt "objectified, as if the rabbi wanted to have bragging rights that he got them to put on tefilln and post their pics somewhere"

But the hardest part for them was that the rabbi told their son who put on tefilln for first time in his life that now he was "bar mitzvah" when meanwhile just a few years before he had worked really hard for his Temple "bar mitzvah".

Obviously this is just  one person's experience, but I took it as a reminder abt trying to be a bit more sensitive with certain folks in the future especially with some of the language and behaviour were used to using since we were bochurim. Ikar is to focus on the mitzvah.  

Figured I would share in case anyone else can benefit.

You can read more about the program here  https://www.mentalhealthfirstaid.org.

Due to covid, the National Council for Mental Wellbeing has pivoted to an online process for taking this course. The virtual delivery of the course has two components.
Part I:  Approximately 2 hours in length, pre-work on your own pace.
Part II: Approximately 6.5 hours in length (including breaks) and is co-lead virtually by MHFA Certified National Instructors 9 am-3:30 pm CST

Since it is all online anyone can join from anywhere in the USA and it will fill up quickly. Upon completion of the training you will receive a certificate valid for three years. Limited spaces are available and early registration will afford you more time to get the pre-work done on your own pace. This is a $75 course, but thanks to a grant it is sponsored and FREE for you to take.

Do you have donors who live in the US or Israel and want to make a tax-deductible donation to your organization? Are you looking to send funds or make a tax deductible donation to a Chabad organization, Yeshiva, seminary, school, camp, or any other charitable organization in the US or Israel? Charity Exchange can help make donations to charities in Canada, Israel, and USA. All donations made using Charity Exchange are eligible for tax-deductible receipt.
 
Charity Exchange is a technology platform that help donors donate globally using a local charitable foundation in their home country. The platform pairs two donors from different countries and matches their donations. Each donor’s donation is exchanged with the other donor, enabling the donor to benefit from a local tax-deductible receipt.

Who can use the Charity Exchange platform?
* Private Donors
* Corporate and Business Donors
* Charities, Foundations and Educational institutions.

Using Charity Exchange can help you:
* Manage all your donations from a single account
* Have access and donate to all registered charities in the countries we operate in
* Track the progress of your donation
* Store and download your tax-deducible receipt under one account

For more information or to open an account visit www.Charity.Exchange

[6/9/21, 8:17:46 PM] ‪+1 (330) 801‑3973‬: I did.

Let me preface by saying that both are great.

But since I switched I've seen multiple pros in Jewish insights.

The idea of Jewish insights is to simply learn a sicha of the Rebbe with its sources (something which most people don't do). So for starters it's a beautiful way to learn a Sicha whether or not you use it for a class. And unlike TS which masterfully weaves in so many layers into each week's topics, JI has a certain beauty of focusing solely and simply on a Sicha. 

A side benefit is that it takes much shorter to prepare for the JI class.

That's my humble take.

[6/14/21, 10:19:52 PM] ‪+1 (305) 790‑6936‬: Hey Friends!
Yesterday was the 40th annual study cycle of Mishneh Torah—the 14-volume compendium of Jewish law by Maimonides commonly just referred to as "Rambam".

*The 41st cycle begins today!* 
Whether you have loads of prior Torah knowledge or none at all now is the perfect time to begin studying Rambam daily.
I would suggest starting with the Daily Mitzvah.
It should take less than 5 minutes a day and by the end of the year you will have knowledge of all the 613 Mitzvot of the Torah!

Let me know if you any other questions about it.

You can find the daily Mitzvah on the daily study app.

Beta for iPhone:
https://testflight.apple.com/join/OeqI7SVm

And on android
https://play.google.com/apps/testing/org.chabad.android.DailyStudy


Enjoy!

[6/28/21, 9:25:59 AM] Chaim Markovits Chaim Hillel: A giluy from your man in Melbourne. 
I think it's relevant to us as shluchim



🛑 *We Need to become Experts in 'Soul Language'*


In Likutei Sichos Vol. 2 Parshas Pinchas pg. 345 the Rebbe explains that since the fires of assimilation are raging in our times, we must speak
*"נשמה ווערטער"*,
words that will touch the soul. 

"מען דארף ניט אויס'טענה'ן זיך מיט זיי מיט שכל'דיקע ויכוחים, ווארום בשעת א שריפה איז ניטא די צייט אויף דעם, און בכלל – ווען עס האנדלט זיך וועגן פקוח נפשות נעמט מען ניט יענעם מיט שכל. 

*מען דארף ריידן מיט רגש - נשמה ווערטער – וואס דערמיט וועט מען אנצינדן דעם פייער וואס ביי זיי .."*

Here the Rebbe negates the idea that we will reach the Millennials or Gen Z by being more sophisticated or academic etc.

Don't think that the youth will be captivated primarily by the intellect of Judaism ..

The Rebbe emphasises that our objective must be to reach their souls, just as it is not the time to engage in intellectual discussions when a fire is raging. *We need to become fluent in "soul-language", not english.*
----------------------------------------
In addition, maybe we can note that 
*רחמנא ליבא בעי*,
Hashem seeks the Heart.
והנה ה' נצב עליו ובוחן כליות *ולב* ..

What is Hashem expecting from all Jews?

Not the אהבת Hashem which is only possible through lofty meditation and deep contemplation but rather, the essential Pinteleh-Yid. See Tanya ch. 18.

As the Alter Rebbe explains, that the Avoda which is realistic to expect from *all* Yidden is through arousing *their already pre-existing "hidden" love.*

Hashem knows that the average Yankel or Shmerel is not a budding philosopher who spends time in deep thought contemplating things of a celestial nature.

The Pinteleh-Yid is *every* Yid's essence. 
שכל איז נאר גילויים.

Hence we expend our energies directed towards everyone's essence. Most people will not be affected by the intellectual depth of an argument. But rather if it feels true to who they are. We bypass the externalities and go straight to the heart.

[6/29/21, 10:55:08 PM] ‪+1 (646) 717‑3279‬: Another dog story 
From an email of Rabbi Wagner:
“The following story, was told to me by Rabbi Dovid Markel, who personally heard the story from the baal hamaaseh:
Eliezer was a young child, growing up in Crown Heights in the mem’s (1980’s). Although, generally speaking, he was a regular Lubavitcher kid, there was one thing unique about him. Because his father was a diamond dealer, the family owned a dog – a Rottweiler – for security reasons. The dog was, by necessity, a big and vicious one, and practically towered over the little boy. When they walked together on the streets of Crown Heights, it was the dog that forcefully led the way, while Eliezer was pretty much dragged along at the end of the leash. Needless to say, anyone else out walking at the same time gave the two of them a wide berth.
Once, Eliezer was out walking with the dog, barely restraining the powerful and energetic dog – as usual -, when suddenly the dog stopped in his place, literally slinking down, with his tail between his feet. Before Eliezer had too much opportunity to wonder at the dog’s uncharacteristic behavior, he suddenly saw the Rebbe pass by right in front of him. Amazed, he turned to the Rebbe and asked: “how is it that you’re not afraid of my dog?” 
The Rebbe smiled to him and replied: “When I was your age, I had an even bigger dog than this.”
Naturally, Eliezer found the Rebbe’s words puzzling, and shared them with his father. His father later shared with him what he had learned from eltere Chassidim, that would shed light on the Rebbe’s words: When the Rebbe was a young child, the streets in Russia were not a safe place for Jewish children (to put it mildly). Therefore, for added security, the Rebbe would take a large dog with him when he went to the beis medrash.”

[7/11/21, 9:24:19 PM] Menachem Aron: *A Dog in 770*


Just a little history & anecdote about the events of that day of the famous visit when Prime Minister M. Begin visited the Rebbe in 1977 (some details may escape me after dozens of years ..).

So basically the U.S. government has a special branch of the Secret Service that secures foreign dignitaries & since this visit was going to be in Brooklyn.. and in Crown Heights.. you can imagine how big of an event it became involving every Security Agency at every level Federal State and local.

So from way back there were a lot of visits in and around 770 from all the security agencies to map out the building, decide on security issues & who can be where & when etc. etc. (rumor had it that ALL person's wearing either one of these Badges had to be cleared ahead of time with the security services in Washington. .....
........


... On the day of the visit itself a small security crew came for the "final sweep" with a sniff dog before they were going to seal off the building to the public. We had to have an argument with them that they cannot go into the Rebbe's room with the dog... or even without..  

They finally accepted it. (In the end I don't think they even went inside the Rebbe's room without the dog, but that I don't remember). 

Around 8 P.M. when Begin was already by Grand Army Plaza (with 20 vehicles etc )  the security did a last minute sweep of the building with a trained dog and the dog sat down - parked itself - in the Mazkirus office .., there's danger here! (and would not move .. now imagine a dog is sitting in Mazkirus not budging an inch .. ..) and you have a major Panic situation, the security team radioed to the Entourage to stop moving forward and wait by the Plaza.

They started to move things around to see what the dog is sniffing .. finally they move a paper bag that contains a thermos inside that the Rebbetzin would send daily tea for the Rebbe, and the thermos glass inside was covered with foil and that foil is also used to hide explosive materials, so the dogs are trained to smell it .. so then as soon as they took the bag out of the building the dog followed the bag and Begin was given the green light...


נכתב לחביבותא ..
ע"י מענדל נאטיק
 היום יום ב' מנחם~אב תשפ"א

So he decided to become shamash at the local shul. Everything was in place and they asked him to sign, but he didn't get the job because he didn't know how to sign his name.

So he went to sell things on the street corner. Business was good and he opened a second location. Then he bought a cart, a truck, a storefront, and before long he was a wealthy owner of a huge chain store.

"If you were so successful without knowing how to sign, imagine if you could sign your name", they exclaimed.

"If I knew how to sign my name, I'd be a shamash at the shul".

[7/18/21, 11:43:26 PM] Menachem Aron: in practice, we consider anyone that claims to be Jewish, Jewish for most mitzvos maasiyos. If they want to marry, bris, bar mitzvah, and some other things, we look into it them.
I always ask people for their Jewish name nad their mothers jewish name, and where their parnents or grnadparents are buried. You can get lots of info from those questions.
Interesting to note that for kvuras yisroel, i was advised by both a rov and the chevra kadisha here that if someone says the yare Jewish, give them kvuras ysireol, and no need to ascertain anything.
Had an actual case where a young girl passed away, and we knew that her mother had been megayer k'din, but was unsure if the giyur was before the girl was born or not. Asking the mother had the potential to make problems, and leopoel we were advised to bury her as a yid, notwithstanding the doubt. I raised that perhaps someone will use the girls matzeiva later down the line as a proof that the family is jewish, rav said not to worry about it.
Have another case now where we have an older guy, holocause survivor but mother died when he was very very young. Says he's jewish. Would take effort to ascertain if Jewish or not. He wants to be cremated. Non jewish granddaughter who takes care of him knows this is not according to jewish law and really wants us to work on conving him to do kvura. Rav says to bury as a yid, him saying he is jeiwsh is sufficient, and we should for sure convince him out of cremation. And interestign to note, rav said, even if he is a goy, still an inyan not to be cremated as the inyan of tzelem elokim applies to goyim's bodies as well according to some opinions.
One last case, a guy wanted to buy a siddur from us. Wasnt sure if he was Jeiwsh. Rav said absolutely no issue, for sure send it to him, and told me that bracha lvatala and saying hashems name in vain only applies to yidden not to goyim. Lepoel, he brought the siddur, sent $180 for it, and also proved that he was Jewish with a certiied letter from an orthodox beth din.
Always ask a rov.

[7/23/21, 9:11:51 AM] Chaim Markovits Chaim Hillel: Reb Mendel here is a beautiful story that underscores your strong conviction of not taking loans…. I don’t know the source of the story!!



Rabbi Avraham Rotenberg was a well-known Gerrer Chasid in Bnei Brak. In around 1957-58, he lived in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn, across from “770,” the Chabad World Headquarters. Though not a Chabadnik, he davened there three times a day. He eventually began to feel at home in 770. He also gradually began to attend the Rebbe's Shabbos farbrengens. At one of these farbrengens, he saw Reb Yankel Lipsker (a prominent Chabad Chassid) approach the Rebbe with a glass of “l’chaim” and requested a blessing for his friend who was in need of a livelihood. The Rebbe responded forcefully and loudly:
"What he needs he has, except that he is used to borrowing and not repaying. He should take upon himself to repay his loans and not borrow anymore, and he will then receive his money directly from God." 
Rottenberg was surprised by the strong tone of the Rebbe’s voice, which was uncharacteristic, and he told himself that he must have heard this exchange by Divine providence, for a purpose. He resolved to never take any loans; come what may, he would do everything to receive directly from G-d. 
Not long afterward, he returned to Israel and began working in the Defense Ministry, in the field of development. Indeed, for years he lived without taking any loans, but when it came time to marry off his children, it became difficult. He managed to marry off his first child, but then found himself completely broke; one of his sons got engaged to be married, but he hadn’t a penny to his name. The night before the wedding, he had to pay a deposit for the bus that would take his guests to the wedding hall, a few hundred shekels, and he didn’t have it. 
The custom among Gerrer Chassidim is that on the morning of the wedding, the groom and his father go to daven wearing the special Shabbos hat, the “spodik". So it was that Rabbi Rottenberg accompanied his son to daven in the Belzer shul on Ben Zakai street in Bnei Brak, with a very troubled heart. He alone knew that he had no way to pay that night for the musicians, the photographer etc. Davening ended, and suddenly he was approached by a respected Chabad chassid, Rabbi Moshe Yaroslavsky (whom he didn’t know), who said, “I see you are wearing a spodik. Are you making a wedding today?”
When Rabbi Rottenberg replied in the affirmative, Rabbi Yaroslavsky said: "I have an envelope with money for you. I just arrived from New York, and before I left, I had a private audience with the Lubavitcher Rebbe. At the end of the audience, the Rebbe took out a large wad of bills and said, ‘You’re going to the Holy Land. When you meet a Jew who’s making a wedding and needs cash, give this to him.’ You’re the first person I’m meeting since I landed that is making a wedding, perhaps the Rebbe was referring to you…”  
(This story appears on page 49 of the book “Abba,” a Hebrew collection of personal experiences with the Rebbe. I will add that I once put out a video with this story, and shortly thereafter I received a phone call from Rabbi Rottenberg’s daughter, a member of the Gerrer community in Tel Aviv, and she confirmed the details to me.)

[7/25/21, 5:47:07 PM] ‪+1 (248) 949‑6210‬: Here's some info on this. Not that your Pete will necessarily be willing to accept it, but this is the metzius:

Min hatorah there is no issue with women learning all of torah. 

At a certain point in history the chachomim took note that women are learning certain areas of torah, and as there was no infrastructure in place to help women in learning it was causing confusion and questions, leading to the opposite of yoras shomayim. (The gemara itself says that Torah can be sam hamaves. One needs proper teachers and role models to help them navigate and be in touch with the truth of torah properly. Women historically did not have that).

As a response to this issue chachomim banned women from studying areas of torah that are relevant to them. As many other takanos, this was a way of protecting against threats to raising a new generation that will be יראים וחרדים לדבר ה'.

In more recent times the tables turned, and now for a women to be frum and have yiras shomayim they now need to be knowledgeable. Meaning the very reason that once prompted the ban on women learning Torah, today leads us to the opposite conclusion - that women must learn Torah.

If you look in the Rebbe's sichos you see that the rebbe is effectively reversing the gzeira against women learning Torah.
[7/25/21, 5:49:14 PM] ‪+1 (323) 770‑3433‬: Fascinating
[7/25/21, 5:56:26 PM] ‪+1 (248) 949‑6210‬: However you explain it, I think it is important to stress that the ban on women learning Torah is not sexist in nature klal uklal. In fact it is in klolei hashas that women are allowed to have an opinion (recorded for posterity in the talmud), have argued with the tanaim of their time, and many times the halacha is like them!

Point being, the reason for the gzeira is a lot more nuanced than "women shouldn't be allowed to have an opinion".

[7/26/21, 10:00:19 AM] ‪+31 6 20045869‬: Anyone here experienced in setting up a free WordPress.org website?
[7/26/21, 10:01:05 AM] Zevi Steinmetz: @15102553121 is king.
[7/26/21, 10:04:19 AM] Shmully Litvin (KY): yes
[7/26/21, 10:22:30 AM] Rabbi Yitzchok Wagner: Happy to help answer any questions.
A few things to make note of (that I can think of off hand)
1. Decent hosting will generally cost you a few $$ a month. (there are free options that are either slower or not that great, or take advanced knowledge) 
2. There is no support, which means when something goes wrong you can post on public forums, and hope someone answers but you don't get free support for any issues.
3. While the core site and many themes and add-ons are free, to add advanced functionality will often mean paying for add ons or better themes.
4. Often plugins and themes get attacks and need to be updated, you need to be on top of updates but at the same time updates can sometimes alter functionality (or have new bugs) so you need to be on top and test them. 

But if you are upto all these things and you know what you are doing, you can really save a lot of money by going this route.
[7/26/21, 10:24:39 AM] Rabbi Yitzchok Wagner: Also, initial setup can take a bit of work, (if someone is willing to let you copy their site it can minimize a lot of it though)

[8/9/21, 1:27:19 PM] ‪+1 (503) 389‑0312‬: Why is it that in general we use a persons  name Ben/ bas the mother but after their passing we say Ben/bas the father?
[8/9/21, 1:36:58 PM] Sholom Vogel (DE): something to do with mothers name used for receiving blessings (kabbala and chassidus explanations *here*) and after passing no longer need for that...
[8/9/21, 1:46:27 PM] ‪+1 (818) 826‑0851‬: By default (Aliyos, after passing) we use the father, based on the possuk למשפחותם לבית אבותם.

The reason why by davening or getting Bracha from a Tzaddik we use mother’s name, is based on the Gemara (שבת סו) which says that all לחשים/tefillos should be said using the mother’s name. The Zohar brings a proof from Dovid Hamelech who said “והודיעה לבן אמתך”, and “אני עבדך בן אמתך”, even though his father was also a Tzaddik.
It also has to do with the fact that one can never be 100% certain in his father’s identity.

It is with great pleasure that we present you with our Chabad of Greenfied Jewish Art Calendar. 
This colorful calendar will brighten your home and office. The Jewish Art Calendar now more than ever is an essential comforting resource for over 800 homes in Greenfield. Amidst all 
the crisis and chaos it is the familiar sense of time and its calming routine; a beautiful Jewish Art 
calendar complete with Shabbat and Holiday times and information on our events here at Chabad. 
There is a Yiddish saying a Mench Tracht un Gut Lacht - a man plan and G-d Laughs. This year 
has truly been a roller coaster. As we approach the new year, the lessons we have learned during the pandemic will continue to influence everything we do at Chabad. We will continue thinking out of the box, we will continue finding new and innovative ways to serve our community, and we will certainly continue focusing on every single individual—reaching out and helping just one person can be the greatest achievement in life. 
Whether you are new to the neighborhood, or born and raised in Greenfield, we welcome 
you to join us in exploring and celebrating our rich Jewish heritage, and to participate in some of 
the ongoing religious, educational and social programs at Chabad or on Zoom.
We wish you a happy and healthy new year. May we all merit good health, happiness, and 
increased prosperity in this upcoming year of 5782. 

Rabbi Yitzi and Miri Goldwasser

It is with great pleasure that we present you with our Chabad of Greenfield Jewish Art Calendar.

calendar complete with Shabbat and Holiday times and information on our events here at Chabad.

has truly been a roller coaster. As we approach the new year, the lessons we have learned during the pandemic will continue to influence everything we do at Chabad. Whether you are new to the neighborhood, or born and raised in Greenfield, we welcome 
you to join us in exploring and celebrating our rich Jewish heritage, and to participate in some of 
the ongoing religious, educational and social programs at Chabad or on Zoom.

[8/17/21, 4:09:02 PM] ‪+1 (612) 275‑6438‬: Isolationism is not a moral or sustainable path for the United States.

A civilized nation must be built upon solid moral foundations. This means that no matter what the immediate situation may be, the country stands by its principles, even if it appears that compromising on principles could bring material gain. Just as every individual plant, animal, and human must grow, an entire country must constantly grow as well, spiritually as well as physically.

When a larger nation chooses to isolate itself from the problems of smaller, less powerful countries, leaving them to struggle with their own problems, this position ends up being to the larger nation’s own detriment. Not only is engagement and involvement with less fortunate nations in the interest of the United States, but it is also its moral G-d-given duty. This stance will ultimately bring greater peace, tranquility, and morality to the U.S. and the rest of the world.

[8/18/21, 9:36:21 AM] ‪+1 (347) 770‑6630‬: The doctor looked at me.

“I think we have to do surgery on your daughter”

She was five years old. She didn’t really understand. She was happy with the sticker at the end. And the promise of a very big prize at the end.

“Don’t worry. It’s routine. We’ve done hundreds of these”

Ha.

My little girl got dressed up in her pajamas. And her blankie. And her sheep. They took her in a ride in a wagon. And she smiled.

Until the stretcher.

They fastened her securely. 

She did not like that one little bit.

They forced her to breathe the sleeping gas. 

She fought it, her eyes searching for me. And wondering why and what was happening. Where was this prize they kept talking about? What happened to the wagon ride?

“You can go now,” they said. “We’ll call you when we’re done”

Go where? I’m not going anywhere.

“Please, sir. Wait in the recovery room.”

I have never felt so helpless. Or alone.

We say that your main shlichus is your family. 

I believe it.

And we say that we are brothers.

I believe that too.

Which means your chaver’s family is also your shlichus.

Which brings mean to my request today - 
A friend of mine is going through a tough time.

His little girl has had surgery - twice - in the recent weeks.

Once for her heart.
 
And then for her brain.

The Rebbe will send brochos. Hashem will help.

The doctors are happy with the scan.

But recovery is long. 6 months estimated. And she needs your help.

The little girl, Sheina Henya Tziporah, needs her Tatti and Mommy - full time.

They can’t do their “other” shlichus - which is running a campus Chabad House in a small town.

You can make sure Sheina Henya Tzipora has her parents when she needs them.

And her parents can have peace of mind to focus on their children.

I don’t often ask you to give. I usually don’t promote campaigns.

This one is special to me.

Please give something if you can.

[8/19/21, 3:14:04 PM] ‪+1 (612) 275‑6438‬: Plain Frozen fruit doesn't need a Hechsher
[8/19/21, 3:14:05 PM] ‪+1 (612) 275‑6438‬: *Bot:* 
Non bug sensitive frozen fruits:
Any frozen cut up fruits without any kosher sensitive additives are acceptable to use without a reliable hashgacha unless it is from China or Israel. Sugar, ascorbic acid and/or citric acid aren’t an issue. 

Bug sensitive frozen fruits:
Can only be used if a) washed well AND b) puréed very finely (hechsher is only the fruit, not that they checked it).

see more at https://sites.google.com/view/kashrusbeintheknow/audio-classes/do-frozen-raw-fruits-and-veggies-need-a-hechsher
(also see link re organic frozen fruit)
Excluding pesach

[8/24/21, 8:07:25 AM] Menachem Aron: Dear Friend,

The High Holidays are almost upon us.

In just a few days, Rosh Hashanah will begin, and we’ll collectively turn the page on our calendars to a new year.

The past year, and in fact 18 months, have been a challenging time for all of us. Rosh Hashanah is a time for us to reset, to start over anew. Every night, we go to sleep, every seven days we begin another week, and every twelve months we begin another year.

These cycles that have been built into our lives are the greatest kindness. They constantly give us a chance to restart, to begin anew, and give things another chance. When we begin a new year, we are given another opportunity to renew our relationships, renew our commitments, and renew our connection to our Judaism.

Rosh Hashanah is not just the first day of the year, but indeed it is the “Head” – “Rosh” in Hebrew – of the year. Much like the head controls the body and its functions, Rosh Hashanah is the day that sets the tone for the coming year.

Beginning with Rosh Hashanah, followed by Yom Kippur, and finally Sukkot, the coming month is packed with special days and unique practices. The enclosed “High Holiday Handbook” and included treats will assist you in kick-starting the new year, and will provide great insight into the meaning, observances, and customs of the upcoming Holiday season.

We take this opportunity to wish you and your loved ones and very happy and sweet new year – a “Shana Tova U’metuka”. May the new year bring much blessing and happiness to your lives and may all your prayers throughout the Holiday season be answered with prosperity and goodness.

Sincerely,

Rabbi Menachem & Shevi Aron

Dearest {contact.first_name},

I am writing to you now to thank you personally for your gift that you made to a Rural Jew.

Here's the story as it happened: 

"Hey do you know anyone Jewish in this area?" 

"Are you seriously asking me if I know anyone Jewish?!"

"Yes, I sure am! In fact, I have been searching for someone Jewish all day. I am about to return home after 8 hours on the ground, asking people all over if they're Jewish or know someone who is."

"Well, you're in luck! I am Jewish. And so is my husband and kids! Would you like to come over and meet them?"

That's how a long day on the road ended. 

We met with Deborah and her husband Joseph, their three children and two dogs. What a great time we had together. 

We're still in touch, and I'll be heading down to visit them again at their home near Greensboro, GA. 

Your partnership brought Deborah and her family a positive Jewish experience. Your partnership ensured that Joseph will not be left behind. 

Thank you!

As it is right before Rosh Hashana and the begining of a new year, I bless y'all with a ksiva vechasima tova, may you be inscribed in to the book of goodness and blessing for a happy and sweet new year.



With love, 

Rabbi Chaim Markovits

[8/26/21, 5:44:52 PM] Mendy Wilschanski: B"H

Chai Elul, 5781

Dear Shliach & Shlucha שיחיו ,

A gut Yom Tov!

As the family of Shluchim & Shluchos continues to grow, so do the Simchas KA" H. With great happiness and profound joy, we took the opportunity to announce the launch of the Keren Hashluchim Simcha Fund during the recent Kinus in Alma Ata on Chof Av. We recognize that every Simcha comes with increased financial obligations, and the new Simcha Fund is designated to help alleviate a small degree of the financial burdens of Shluchim.

In addition to the new Simcha fund, the Keren provides grants for personal Yom Tov expenses and financial support for Shluchim in times of emergency and crisis. We are working diligently to expand the funding to other personal needs for Shluchim and the growth of Shlichus. We look forward to sharing more grant opportunities as they become available.

The Keren is now accepting applications for the Simcha Fund from Yud Aleph Menachem Av 5781 – Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5782. Shluchim who have merited to have a new baby, celebrate a Bar Mitzvah, or make a Chasunah during this period, are invited to submit a grant application at kerenhashluchim.org.

Eligibility for grants is determined using qualifying metrics established and overseen by representatives from the Keren Hashluchim and Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch Vaad. At this time, the funds are available for full-time Shluchim, active in Avodas Hashlichus twelve months a year, and generate their Parnassah through these activities.

Visit kerenhashluchim.org for more information and available grant opportunities.

With blessings for a Ksiva V'Chasimah Tova to the entire family of Shluchim, Anash, and Klal Yisroel.

Sincerely,
Rabbi Moshe Kotlarsky

[8/31/21, 12:09:42 PM] Shmully Litvin (KY): Few Thoughts, in no order:

1) Make sure you and your chazzan (and whatever other anash/family/shluchim) know what songs you are singing where, the tunes, and participate.

2) go over the davening with the chazzan where you will talk about what's happening (if you want to do this) for example explaining zicheonos, shofaros. Also what you plan on doing in English.
3) make a list of the pesichas, and write in who you want to make sure has, so you honor appropriately. The list should have the page number, so you know when it's coming and you stop shmoozing and avoid awkward pauses while the chazzan waits for the Aron to be open.
4) have reading material for the crowd, JLI flyers, insights, testimonials, davening is long and good chance they will look at it.
5) calendars, flyers, Kippas on the swag table
6) you could choose to dedicate sections of davening to various donors of sections
7) if you don't have a page display, announce pages often. 
8) if you are allowed to covidly do this, and have anyone else with you, Bochurim, wife, etc, have them watch sections of the shul to make sure ppl know what they are doing.
9) a dear shliach mentor would during avoda have posters and props to show the different stages of avoda. Though he didn't show the mikva dips. 

That's my first brain dump

[8/31/21, 10:42:54 PM] Meir Pape: Artscrolls book contains a biography of all תנאים ואמוראים, a traslation of שלש עשרה מידות שהתורה נדרשת. Basically lots of irrelevant information. Looks like they just needed to print something for the siyum.

In his classic original style he writes simply and articulated how the Talmud mindset works, meaning he goes through history and development, darchei halomud, the gemara's shakla vetaria style, how the analysis methods of Gemara differs from common acamedics, what to expect as in Rashi tosfos, etc. Basically perfect for a learned person with no prior Talmud study experience, to take him from a stranger to Talmud to knowing what to expect.

[9/1/21, 6:52:35 PM] ‪+1 (503) 389‑0312‬: Tayere Chaveirim,

As we stand just a few days before Rosh Hashanah, I would like to share with you two very special answers I merited to receive from the Rebbe, 32 years ago, in Elul 5749 (1989).

Just to give some background: It is well-known that the Rebbe requested the establishment of The Shluchim Office 34 years ago, at a Farbrengen during the Kinus Hashluchim 5747. The purpose, the Rebbe said, was to be a מקום מרכזי to advise and serve the Shluchim in fulfilling their Shlichus. The opening of this central office took some time and in 5749, Rabbi Chadokov and the Vaad Hashluchim asked that I run The Shluchim Office under his direct supervision. 

That year, the Shluchim Office launched several major activities, such as: ‘Shluchim Placement’ -  matching Shluchim and Yungeleit, as well as placing chazzanim for Yomim Noraim and bochurim for yomim toivim throughout the year; ‘Project Talmud’ - arranging learning retreats and preparing classes for Shluchim; ‘General Duch’ - making it easy for Shluchim to report their activities to the Rebbe; ‘How-To Guides’ - offering step-by-step guidance for organizing events, camps and many other peulos; beautiful Yomtov guides and flyers, and much more.

One of our very first activities was a campaign to encourage Shluchim around the world to place an ad in their local newspapers in preparation for Rosh Hashanah. The ad featured a message of the Rebbe on Rosh Hashanah alongside a beautiful picture of the Rebbe, and an invitation to reach out to their local Chabad House.

In short, the message explained that Adam HaRishon (the first man) was created alone to demonstrate how one person equals a whole world. So too, each Jew has the capacity and duty to bring fulfilment to himself and the entire world. (You can see a scanned copy of the full ad below.)

1. On 15 Elul 5749, I sent in a copy of the ad to the Rebbe, and wrote that the ad had been sent to Shluchim around the world to publish in their local newspapers.

I was zoiche to receive the following response from the Rebbe:

*ויהא בהצלחה רבה*
*והזמ"ג [והזמן גרמא]*
*וכוח"ט [וכתיבה וחתימה טובה]*
*אזכיר עה"צ [על הציון]*

A free translation:
*And it should be with much success*
*And the time is now appropriate*
*And may you be written and sealed for a good year*
*I will mention it at the tziyun [of my father in law, the Rebbe]*

2. The following week, in the Days of Selichos, The Shluchim Office placed the same ad in the New York Times, together with a list of Chabad Houses around the world.

I gave in a copy of the ad in the New York Times together with a letter asking for a brocho in everything.

ומבקשים את ברכת כ"ק אדמו"ר שליט"א להצלחה בכל

The Rebbe answered:

*ורבה כפשוט והזמ"ג [והזמן גרמא]*
*וכתיבה וחתימה טובה*
*וכן בכל המצורף בזה*
*ודלעתיד*
*אעה"צ [אזכיר על הציון]*

A free translation (the bold words are the Rebbe’s):
I wrote: We ask for the Rebbe’s blessing for success in everything. 
The Rebbe continued: *“in abundance, of course*
*And the time is now appropriate.*
*And may you be written and sealed for a good year*
*And [the above also applies] to all that's enclosed in [your] letter as well as to future [activities]*
*I will mention it at the tziyun [of my father in law, the Rebbe].”*

The Rebbe’s answers show us the importance of sharing the Rebbe’s message of Rosh Hashana with everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike. I’m sure you will be able to use this message to inspire yidden in your community. May we all give tremendous nachas ruach to the Rebbe, now, “ודלעתיד”.

Wishing you much hatzlocho in your shlichus, and in the words of the Rebbe, “וכתיבה וחתימה טובה”.

B'yedidus,

Rabbi Gedalya Shemtov
The Shluchim Office

[9/3/21, 1:05:11 PM] ‪+1 (917) 474‑3257‬: Other symbolic foods include dates, leeks, beets and carrots. The Hebrew word for “date” is tamar, symbolizing our request she-yitamu oyveinu, “that our enemies be consumed.” The Aramaic term for “leeks” is karti, symbolizing our request she-yikartu oyveinu, “that our enemies be cut off.” The Aramaic word for “beets” is silka, symbolizing our request she-yistalku oyveinu, “that our enemies disappear.” The Yiddish word for “carrots” is mehrin (“multiply”), symbolizing our wish that our merits should increase.

[9/5/21, 9:06:27 AM] ‪+1 (612) 275‑6438‬: *Head of the Year- Cherish Each Moment*

It is explained in various sources in Chassidus that Rosh HaShanah is called the head of the year rather than the beginning of the year, because its relation to the other days of the year parallels the relation of the head to the body and the other organs.

Just as the vitality of all the organs is subsumed in the head, and this then finds overt expression in the fact that the vitality of every particular organ is drawn down from the head, so, too, Rosh HaShanah comprises within itself the vitality of all the days of the forthcoming year. They are all subsumed in it in potential form, and eventually their vitality branches out into individual days and becomes apparent.

It may be assumed that this is one of the reasons why we have been earnestly urged to be exceedingly vigilant in cherishing time on Rosh HaShanah — for the hours and the minutes of these days are “all-inclusive”....


(Reprinted with permission from “I Will Write It In Their Hearts” (SIE), translated from a letter which served as an introduction to the kuntres for Rosh HaShanah, 5711)

[9/6/21, 2:31:11 PM] ‪+1 (805) 668‑1024‬: Hope this is helpful to someone. 

Shofar Talk 5782 

Waiters. Usually in a restaurant they approach you and ask is everything ok. In a kosher restaurant serving jews they have a different question. Is anything ok? 

Sometimes it seems that we are always getting the short end of the Shofar. 

Take this Shofar. Show them the Shofar.  What's it's story. Sitting on shelf. Gathering dust. Ignored all year. Plates in and out. Candlesticks come ago. Shofar is untouched. 

Until RH. On RH we take this Shofar and we blow it. And it's purpose is realized. Its so happy that it plays a part in helping us become better people and more connected Jews. When we blow the Shofar we infuse it with purpose direction and meaning. YOU MAKE IT SPECIAL! 

What's about the Shofar is interesting? Its a microcosm of all strata of existence. 

It simply is. Like the planets rock soil. 
It grew once on the head of a ram. Has that aspect of plant life about it. Grows. 
It was part of an animal. Microcosm of the animal kingdom. 
But it's meaningless and all of reality is meaningless until you blow it and infuse life into it. 

You are a Shofar blower. When your in class and you help a friend you infuse your classroom with Gdly light and goodness. 

When you light Shabbat candles or put up a mezuzah you are imbuing your home with light. 

And tomorrow when you come to hear Shofar you are bringing light and goodness to your year and throughout Isla Vista. 

Remember the game Pokemon Go. All these characters are waiting for you to collect them. 

All across our family life we meet persons elements waiting to be elevated by you. The Shofar blower. 

Story of the construction worker who drives by the trench he's supposed to fill. 

Spectator vs player. 

Rosh Hashanah is time to embrace our mission. It's up to you to blow the short end of the Shofar and bring light to ask of your reality. 

Story of Shirley Chisholm. Opportunity to help so many. 

Message of RH. You matter. YOU are the only one who can fill your reality with Hashemliness.

Tzom Gedaliah is shrouded in mystery, even the date of the murder of Gedaliah is debated amongst our Sages – whether it happened on Rosh HaShana and was pushed to the 3rd of Tishrei or it actually occurred on the 3rd of Tishrei.

[9/10/21, 2:52:05 PM] ‪+1 (928) 600‑6331‬: SHVITZING IS GOOD FOR YOU

We are still on a high from a beautiful Rosh Hashana. Especially during these challenging times, it is especially meaningful to to find safe ways to gather on these holy days.

I first felt that energy of the Holidays Monday afternoon when 18 volunteers came out to help us move supplies to 111 Place for the holidays. There was lots of shvitzing as hundreds of Machzorim, synagogue furniture, supplies for the kids program, and a complete Rosh Hashana dinner for 100 was loaded on car trunks and trucks.

Quite the Labor Day! :)

The next day it was our family's turn for shvitzing as we walked back to our house in Morrisville after Shul ended. (Thankfully, most of the 5 mile walk was along the Greenway!) The highlight of the walk was bumping into some Jewish bikers along the way who had not yet heard the Shofar. Together, we stood there, quite sweaty, sharing a holy moment together.

What's the meaning behind all this sweating on the Holy Day, my kids wanted to know?

A perspective became clear that night.

I was thanking a community member who had recently "upped" their monthly donations to Chabad of Cary. She responded with these powerful words:

"I realized that if I don't feel it each month, that's a sign I'm probably not giving enough. Obviously, it shouldn't break us...but it should stretch us a bit and not just feel like the phone bill or something else I hardly notice each month."

Wow. I had never quite thought about Mitzvot in that manner. When it comes to a physical workout, it's often said that the real exercise begins when we begin to shvitz. (Or in the words of Muhammad Ali "I don't start counting the sit-ups until it hurts.") Here she was saying the very same thing about a workout of the soul!

And that makes sense. Certainly every Mitzvah is significant. Each additional good deed connects us to G-d and brings holiness and positivity to the world. But when a Mitzvah results in toiling -- whether physical, emotional, or mental -- that's a sign we're truly serving Hashem. These are acts that transform us. 

Some examples come to mind:

Tzedaka beyond our comfort zone

Learning Torah in a deeper/longer manner where we really have to mentally exert ourselves

Reaching out with love to someone with whom one has a difficult time getting along...or forgiving someone even when its incredibly difficult to do so

Praying with a heightened focus and intensity.

Or any physical shvitzing for a Mizvah...not hard to do when the temps are in the 90's!

Throughout the year, we will all be "shvitzing" for one thing or another.  "Man is born to toil" (Job 5:7) tells us that there will always be that "grind" in life.

The question is only "in what will we toil? What will be the types of things we labor and sweat over? Will it be over positive, or G-d forbid, negative things?

The seven days days Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur set the tone for rest of the year.  What better way to spend these days than by "shvitzing for a Mitzvah" and telling Hashem "This is how we want to spend the year!"

May Hashem bless us all with a healthy and sweet year...a year in which all our shvitzing is only for simchos and Mitzvos!
[9/10/21, 2:52:10 PM] ‪+1 (928) 600‑6331‬: Here is one
[9/10/21, 2:52:48 PM] ‪+1 (928) 600‑6331‬: LET'S GO BACK

"Lumir zich umkeren, Yiddelach!"

So goes the refrain of a lovely Yiddish song, sung in the attached video by my talented brother, Benny.

The melody, written by the beloved Yiddish songwriter, Reb Yomtov Erlich, is a call to his fellow Jews, "We have to turn around, Yidden!" He paints a lyrical picture of a group of Jews enjoying a train ride to an exciting destination when one of them discovers that the train is racing in the wrong direction. In great concern, he goes from person to person, informing the whole group of the problem, encouraging them all, "Lumir zich umkeren, Yiddelach."

It's a simple message, a metaphor for a Jewish person encouraging others to Teshuva, but there is added depth to his words: "Lumir zich umkeren Yiddelach."

1. "Lumir": His words are an invitation, not a decree. He doesn't say, "Repent! Return!" He says, "We have to turn around. Let's do this together." And that's why they listen to him.

2. "Lumir zich": The man encouraging a turnaround is no outsider. He is no preacher, speaking from a lofty perch. He is right there with them all, in the thick of the problem. If they don't decide to turn around, he doesn't reach his destination either. His call for a course correction is more than a directive; it is a plea from the depths of his heart. And that's why they listen to him. 

3. "Umkeren": He calls not for repentance but for return. He doesn't encourage improvement; he encourages return. The implication is a subtle but crucial one. He isn't asking anyone to change and become anything they aren't already, or haven't been in the past. He is simply urging them to be true to themselves, to return to their real selves and to align their lives with their deepest, truest identity: their Jewish souls. The Neshama. He doesn't beckon for them to follow him on a new, unfamiliar path; he simply points out that when you come from greatness, and you've strayed, you need only turn around and go back to where you came from. That's why they listen to him. 

4. "Yiddelach": He calls his fellow Jews just that - his fellow Jews. He uses a term of endearment, "Yiddelach." He encourages them to Teshuva not because of who he wants them to be but because of who he knows they are. His invitation for everyone to pull together and turn things around is an invitation driven by his love for his fellow Jew. He is motivated not by a desire to point out the other's flaws but by a desire to bring out the other's greatest strengths and deepest qualities. And that's why they listen to him.

***

On this Shabbat Shuva, the Shabbat of Return, let us grab each other's hands and hearts, speak to one another as brothers, see the beauty in every soul, and say from a place of real concern: "Lumir zich umkeren Yiddelach!"

We come from a good place of Torah, Mitzvot, and lives filled with sanctity and purpose. As Benny says, come on Yiddelach, vámonos. Let's turn around and go back to where we came from.

Shabbat Shalom, good Shabbos and Gmar Chatima Tova!

Rabbi Eli Friedman
Chabad of Calabasas

[9/14/21, 12:47:17 AM] Mendy Wilschanski: Can't speak to this particular Vort but I heard a nice way to explain it... Obviously it has to be to the right person someone who will be Mekabel it etc... 

When the Chachomim established Minyan, there was no way for woman to join together with the men. (If they wanted to do their own that was fine but Halacha had no way to be in the same place as the men).

In order to invite the woman in, they established the Mechitzah...

If you look at it from this perspective it turns the Mechitzah into being inviting thing, as opposed to being dividing...

[9/15/21, 8:45:40 AM] Dinarman Yishei: Anyone know a YY Jacobson story he said 2-3 years ago, of a famos kiruv man in EY whose son passed away. And the boys that he would work with decided to keep one Shabbos in his memory? 
Looking for more details
[9/15/21, 8:53:35 AM] Dinarman Yishei: Got it. Here it is.
[9/15/21, 8:53:38 AM] Dinarman Yishei: Story - Rabbi Chaim Weintraub from Kiryat Shmuel is involved in outreach,
particularly with youth, known as ‘kids at risk.’ These teenagers have often left
their homes and traditions, and are vulnerable to many different influences,
sometimes harmful.
Rabbi Weintraub is known to be very active with these youngsters, he embraces
them and hangs out with them, loves them.
A little while ago he was celebrating his sons upshernish – haircutting.
A few days after, the child complained to his teacher that he had a headache, the
teacher told the child to lay in the cot next door and take a nap. The teacher went
in sometime later to check on him, she saw immediately that something was
wrong, and it was determined that the boy had returned his soul to his maker, he
went to sleep and never woke up.
It was devastating beyond words, the Rabbi and his wife and the siblings were
sitting shiva for this angelic boy. People came to visit, the pain unbearable, the
grief incomprehensible, the mystery infinite.
Who came to pay a shiv a call? A bunch of these teenagers, many of them
tattooed, many with piercings all over their body, many with different
experiences over the years... They sat with their beloved Rabbi, and as they were
about to leave, they turned to Rabbi Weintraub and they said ‘Rabbi we wan to
pay tribute to you and your little boy, so we want to tell you, that this coming
Shabbat we are going to observe, we won’t drive, we won’t smoke. We will
celebrate and observe this Shabbat in your sons honor.
A few people who were there in the home and overheard this told the Rabbi
‘Rabbi, that was so cheap, after all you have done for them, all they can o for you
is tell you that they will keep ONE Shabbat? Maybe for the rest of the year, for 6
months, for a few years.. One Shabbos? They are going to keep one Shabbos, 24
hours for you? Very unbecoming….
Rabbi Weintraub turned to his visitors and said: ‘How much would I pay to have
my little boy with me JUST FOR ONE SHABBOS, just so that when I come home
Friday he will come running to me and I will hold him and put him on my lap and
hold him as we sing Sholom Aleichem… To cuddle him up in his blanket after the
Friday night dinner, to walk with him to Shul on Shabbat morning… What do you
think I would pay to have just one more Shabbos with him?
I would pay absolutely everything he said… all my belongings, everything… Just to
have my boy one last shabbos here on earth, so friends don’t you understand –
this Shabbos our father in heaven is going to have 8 of his children together with
him the entire Shabbos. Do you know the pleasure that G-d will have this
Shabbos? Because 8 of his teenagers who were lost, who have wondered far away
are going to come back to their father in heaven and you have the nerve to say
‘Eh, just one Shabbos!” Do you know the Nachat that G-d will have this Shabbos
when he embraces these 8 teenagers who will celebrate Shabbat with him?!
Don’t denigrate it, realize the awesomeness. These are the words of a griefstricken
father at the Shiva call with these guests.
It taught me that we must look at ourselves and know who we are, we don’t
understand the great joy that G-d has when we say ‘Father I want to spend time
with you.’

[9/23/21, 9:38:59 PM] Shmully Litvin (KY): There is Incorporating, which is filing as a non profit with your state, which needs articles of incorporation, and a form with your secretary of state. Kentucky is $8 bucks. Others not so much.

You need an EIN, which is free online

You then need to file with the IRS form I think 1240, to become a 501c3. It's a long form, which needs bylaws, a bunch of questions about what you do, narrative, 3 yr projected budget. For a regular charity it cost 600 bucks to file, for a 99ez it cost 400.

I use A2ZFilings.com, Shai Goldstein, multiple times. His entire sales pitch. He has a 100% track record with creating 501c3. Tell him I sent you. 

He is knowledgeable in the language giving all authority to the shliach, especially if you nebach loy aleinu have a board.

[9/26/21, 6:56:20 PM] ‪+1 (408) 910‑2034‬: What are these "hut" like structures I see in our neighborhood? The answer to this question is what you are seeing is called a Sukkah! in short, it's a traditional Jewish structure, assembled during the Sukkot holiday. In physical terms, it's a hut-like structure in which one eats and communes during Sukkot. Traditionally, sukkahs are simple tents or basic structures.

Sukkot is a little like Thanksgiving. It is a festival for giving thanks for many things, like food and shelter. The holiday celebrates the farmer's yearly harvest, which takes place in the fall. And commemorates the biblical story of the Jews' escape from Egypt. This is a wonderful and joyous holiday and I hope for those that were wondering this helped explain. The holiday concludes on the evening on September 28th...

Chag Sameach to all who are celebrating! 
(Happy Festival)

For more information on this holiday, including stories and sukkot recipes, check out chabadof×××.com/sukkot

פרשת בראשית. 

*ויהי ערב ויהי בקר יום שני* (א,ה)

שאלות:

א) למה לא נאמר כי טוב ביום שני?

ב) ביאור הטעם דגיהנם נברא *ביום שני* דוקא?

ג) ביאור הזהר דיש גיהנם של *שלג*, ועד גיהנם של *אש*, ומהו החילוק ביניהם?

ד) רמז בהנל *בהשם* גיהנם.

לקוטי לוי יצחק הערות לזהר בראשית ע׳ רלז ואילך
ילקוט לוי ייצור עה״ת בראשית סימן יג

[10/3/21, 6:40:39 PM] ‪+1 (818) 826‑0851‬: Our version is a bit different:

We used to have a Mentsh Club as well (pre-covid), once a month, with men getting together, eating, socialize and learn something on the Parsha.

But the chevreh were saying that they wanted something more structured, so after Tishrei last year when we restarted, it morphed into our weekly Tequila and Tanya class.

We have a roster, and each week one guy sponsors lchaim and dinner (they choose the menu), everyone socializes for about half an hour, then I give a shiur, and then everyone sticks around for about another hour and continues socializing.

As the months went by and more people started showing up, it mamesh became a mini-community, and b”h seeing tremendous hatzlacha.

[10/5/21, 11:14:00 PM] ‪+1 (716) 650‑0613‬: This extraordinary idea was explained by the Lubavitcher Rebbe in an answer dated 4 Teves, 5743 (writing to someone who was trying to convince his father not to request his own cremation). Here is the summation: Even as a soul departs, the body still has some form of life; as long as the body does not completely decompose, part of the soul still clings to it. When someone burns the body, it is akin to burning part of the soul which is still connected to the body. In that sense, it is like burning a living person. But not burning the entire person, only part of him, which is extremely painful and cruel. Even agreeing to do it to yourself is wrong and cruel. The fact that many do this does not justify it. Would anyone justify burning, G-d forbid, living people because thousands of Nazis, including scientists, merchants, family members, burnt living people?

[10/6/21, 1:00:31 PM] ‪+1 (862) 812‑6224‬: Depending what's more important. Convenience or money. 
Some rather headache free and pay more monthly, some rather save and deal with the hassle of maintenance and selling. 
The cheaper way is definitely used, and the most expensive way is definitely lease. But with used comes potential maintenance issues you need to deal with.
The best deal is to buy a 2 or 3 year old car, so you get the discount of used but still pretty new with no issues. It's still going to be more expensive than a 5 or 10 year old car. 
Don't buy older than 10 years, or over 100k miles. You'll end up spending more on repairs, making it not worth while. 

When buying used, don't buy to keep. Hold for couple years and sell. If you're lucky, and buy and sell right. You'll end up not spending much at all for the car. You can just spend a thousand dollars or so for having a car for 2 or 3 years or maybe less.

The following is the recollection of the conversation that Rabbi Yosef Posner had with Rabbi Nochem Kaplan, Menahel of Vaad Rabonei Lubavitch (VRL), on 5 Adar II, 5779. It was pursuant to a letter which several Illinois Shluchim had sent to VRL asking whether the ban on Hisachdus products was still in force:

VRL will not issue a written reply, but the following points were put forth:

1) Generally, when a Gezaira is made for a reason, once the reason is gone the Gezaira is gone on its own. In this case, things seems to have been changed substantially.

2) It does not appear that the Rebbe wanted this in the first place, but once the Rabonim declared it…

3) Before his petira, Rabbi Zalman Shimon Dvorkin was asked what will be with this Gezaira and he said it would be botul on its own once he is no longer bein hachaim.

4) VRL is not ready to take any action to be mevatel the Gezaira at this time.

They recommend that each Rov decide what is appropriate for the needs of his local community.

[10/12/21, 12:18:15 PM] ‪+1 (216) 496‑0014‬: FYI this may be cringeworthy and frustrating at first. but it is very worthwhile in the long run. (obviously dont give it to someone who is tone deaf) People will feel it is their minyan that they have to make. Depending on your crowd, you can have them share a/the Dvar Torah/thought for that week. You can advertise it sometimes before hand. It'll take work to guide them to different places but this has many gains even beyond your minyan. 

If youre crowd is into the sermon, make sure you prepare a good one. dont wing it. and yes people can tell. if you are not a naturally good speaker, put a lot of effort into this. 

If youre crowd is NOT into the speeches, find ways to skip it. Don't let your ego of wanting to speak get in the way.
